notes: This paper does not describe a preceramic polymer in the traditional sense. The preceramic paper is fabricated using BaTiO3 ceramic filler (d50 = 1.2 um) embedded in a cellulosic pulp fiber matrix with organic additives (anionic and cationic starch ester, polyacrylamide-derivative Percol 121L, thermoplastic binder Planatol AD95). The organic components serve as sacrificial binder/template, not as a Si-based polymer precursor to ceramic. BaTiO3 content in preceramic papers ranged from 70 to 80 vol%. Relative sintering densities ranged from 68.7% (70 vol%) to 86.2% (80 vol% calendered). Piezoelectric coefficients: d33 = 39.1-77.3 pC/N; d31(MD) = -16.3 to -49.7 pC/N; d31(CD) = 15.5-55.7 pC/N. Relative permittivity at room temperature ranged from 660.8 to 1514.1 depending on porosity. Curie temperature ~120 C. Multilayer ceramics fabricated by warm lamination at 80 C and 8.3 MPa. Grain size midpoint reported as 800 nm (fine-grained matrix); range noted as fine ~0.8 um and coarse ~20 um. Modulus midpoint reported as 45 GPa; range 30-60 GPa.
source: Menge et al. - 2018 - Paper-Derived Ferroelectric Ceramics A Feasibility Study

notes: This is a review article covering multiple classes of silicon-based preceramic polymers (polysilanes, polycarbosilanes, polysiloxanes, polysilazanes, polysilylcarbodiimides). No single polymer is characterized in detail; most descriptors are general or class-level. Key points: (1) Kumada rearrangement converts polydimethylsilane to polycarbosilane at ~400C; (2) polysilsesquioxanes RSiO1.5 are highly cross-linked and give high ceramic yields; (3) metal alkoxide modification (Zr, Hf) strongly increases crosslinking; (4) carbon content in PDCs controlled by organic substituents R1/R2 at Si; (5) chlorine impurities from chlorosilane synthesis shift Si3N4 crystallization onset ~200C higher and affect creep behavior; (6) Nicalon SiC fibers derived from polycarbomethylsilane pyrolysis at 1100C in argon; (7) silicon diimide (from ammonolysis of SiCl4) converts to amorphous Si3N4 at ~1000C releasing NH3.
source: Mera and Ionescu - 2013 - Silicon‐Containing Preceramic Polymers

notes: This is a review article covering the broad field of polymer-derived ceramics (PDCs), not a single polymer system. Multiple polymer classes are discussed: polysilanes, polycarbosilanes, polysiloxanes, polysilazanes, polysilylcarbodiimides, and polyborosilazanes. Grain size of 2 nm is the midpoint of the reported 1-3 nm nanodomain size range. Commercial fiber data tabulated includes Siboramic (Bayer, amorphous, specific weight 1.85 g/cm3), Sylramic (Dow Corning, crystalline, specific weight 3.1 g/cm3), HiNicalon (Nippon Carbon, partially crystalline, 2.7 g/cm3), and Ube SA (Ube Industries, crystalline, 3.1 g/cm3). Yajima process described: poly(dimethylsilane) -> poly(methyl hydrido carbosilane) via Kumada rearrangement at 400C -> melt-spun fibers -> crosslinked -> pyrolyzed at 1100C in argon to SiC fibers. Metal-functionalized precursors described using Al, Ti, V, Zr, Hf alkoxides. 3D printing and additive manufacturing technologies for PDCs also discussed.

notes: Polymer S2 is -[Ph(CH3)Si-NCN]n-, a carbon-rich polysilylcarbodiimide precursor yielding carbon-rich SiCN PDC ceramics. microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Non-modified PDC is amorphous at 1000 °C per XRD and manufacturer datasheet. Expected SiCN ceramic but significant oxygen content observed by XPS, attributed to PSZ moisture sensitivity. Al2O3-modified PDCs show residual low-intensity Al2O3 XRD peaks indicating partial reaction. Si3N4 peaks absent in XRD of 15 wt% Si3N4-modified PDC indicating full reaction. Secondary phase formation (e.g., silicon oxynitride) suggested. Si(2p) XPS peak shifts toward Si-O in Si3N4-modified samples.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Baseline PDC (no filler): hardness ~4.1 GPa, modulus ~73 GPa, KIC not explicitly stated for baseline but JIC ~0.29 kJ/m2. Best Al2O3 (6 wt%): modulus ~113 GPa (55% improvement), hardness ~3× baseline. Best Si3N4 (2 wt%): modulus ~4% improvement, hardness ~50% improvement, KIC ~7 MPa·m0.5 (~1.5× baseline), JIC ~0.75 kJ/m2 (~2.5× baseline). CNTs (1 wt%): modulus 50% improvement, hardness ~9.8 GPa (2.5× baseline). Fracture toughness measured by micro-indentation crack length method (Antis et al.). Solid density of non-modified PDC estimated at 1980 ± 76 kg/m3.

notes: Elemental compositions reported in the table are for the resulting PDC ceramics (after pyrolysis at 1000 °C), not the preceramic polymer itself. PSZ20 ceramic composition (atomic %): Si 35.6, C 29.7, N 20.7, O 14.0. Pyrolysis performed under isostatic pressure of 30 MPa in nitrogen. Crosslinking first at 150 °C for 15 min, then ramped to 400 °C at 2 °C/min with 4-hour hold, then ramped to 1000 °C at 2 °C/min with 4-hour hold, cooled at 2 °C/min. TGA used argon atmosphere at 10 °C/min as a modified version of the pyrolysis protocol. Fillers explored: Al2O3 nanoparticles (13 nm), Si3N4 nanopowder (<50 nm), and multiwalled CNTs (NC7000, avg diameter 9.5 nm). Both Al2O3 and Si3N4 identified as active fillers. Mechanical properties (hardness and modulus) correlate positively with apparent density.

notes: This paper is a computational/modelling study of polymer-derived amorphous nitride ceramics (a-Si3N4, a-Si3B3N7, a-SiNO, a-SiCN) using DFT and ab initio molecular dynamics. It does not characterize a specific preceramic polymer precursor directly. Model sizes range from 104 to 448 atoms. Free internal energy relative to crystalline phases: a-SiO2 ~0.04 eV/atom, a-Si2N2O ~0.23 eV/atom, a-Si3N4 ~0.27 eV/atom (180 kJ/mol). Ab initio MD simulations performed at 800-2600 C. a-SiCN composition modeled as Si40C40N40. Carbon non-solubility in a-Si3N4 or stoichiometric a-SiCN supported by energy calculations. Dominant topological defect in a-Si3N4 is four-fold coordinated N (~7% of N atoms); ~4% two-fold coordinated N; ~4% five-fold coordinated Si; ~1% three-fold coordinated Si.

notes: This paper does not describe a preceramic polymer. It describes a preceramic paper method using elemental inorganic powders (Ti, TiC, Si, C) with organic papermaking additives (cellulose pulp, ionic starches, polyacrylamide) to fabricate Ti3SiC2 MAX phase ceramics. The organic additives contribute 17.3 wt% residual amorphous carbon after heat treatment (TGA under Ar to 800 °C, heating rate 300 K/h). Sintering performed in flowing Ar at 1300–1600 °C for 1 h, heating/cooling rate 180 K/h. Porosity of paper-derived samples typically 35–55%. thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: TGA showed three mass loss events: first below 250C (THF decomposition), second above 250C (NH3 and methyl radicals), third around 500C (mineralization begins, H2 evolution). Heated to 1000C at 2C/min then to 1500C at 5C/min with 5 min hold, under flowing UHP N2. XRD pyrolysis experiments performed to 1600C at 1C/min with 1h hold in various atmospheres.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal (crosslinking at ~180C under inert atmosphere) or chemical (dicumyl peroxide radical initiator at room temperature under inert atmosphere)

molecular_weight.measurement_method: GPC (Viscotek MAX TDA 302 tetra-detector); note: instrument lower limit of detection ~1000 g/mol, so value is an average with standard deviation ~50 g/mol

backbone_architecture.description: Linear polyvinylsilazane network formed via ammonolysis of vinyltrichlorosilane in THF; Si-N-Si backbone with pendant vinyl groups on silicon

microstructural.ceramic_phase: SiCN (atmosphere-dependent: alpha-Si3N4 dominant under N2 or NH3; alpha-SiC dominant under Ar, He, or H2)
microstructural.phase_composition_notes: At 1600C: NH3 atmosphere yields alpha-Si3N4 (major) + trace beta-Si3N4; N2 atmosphere yields alpha-Si3N4 (major) + beta-Si3N4 (minor), no SiC; Ar atmosphere yields alpha-SiC Moissanite-6H (major) + alpha-Si3N4 (minor); He and H2 atmospheres yield only alpha-SiC. Crystalline phases form at 1600C.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Polymer capable of forming free-standing monolithic pucks and drawn fibers (10-30 micrometers diameter)

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: alpha-Si3N4 (JCPDS 41-360), beta-Si3N4 (JCPDS 33-1160), alpha-SiC Moissanite-6H (JCPDS 29-1131); phases depend on pyrolysis atmosphere

notes: Polymer synthesized via ammonolysis of vinyltrichlorosilane in THF. Pale yellow viscous liquid with density ~1.0 g/cm3. Limited shelf life (1 day as neat polymer; extended by storage as PVSZ/THF solution under N2 in freezer). Crosslinking at ~180C under inert atmosphere or with 1 wt% dicumyl peroxide. Puck fabricated by heating to 350C at 2C/min with 1h dwell under N2. Fibers pyrolyzed to 1000C at 2C/min with 1h hold under N2. Elemental composition data in table is for ceramic char (1100C), not the preceramic polymer. Ceramic yield >85% is higher than Ceraset Polysilazane 20 (~82%) and HPZ (~60%). XRD crystalline phases identified at 1600C. RGA performed in UHP helium to 800C at 1C/min.
source: Reutenauer et al. - 2011 - Synthesis and characterization of polyvinylsilazane as a precursor for Si3N4 based ceramic materials

notes: This paper is a review of Ultra-High Temperature Ceramic Matrix Composite (UHTCMC) fabrication techniques (hot pressing, SPS, PIP, CVI, RMI, sol-gel, slurry infiltration, microwave sintering, flash sintering, etc.). It does not describe or characterize a specific preceramic polymer. No polymer-specific descriptors such as elemental composition, bonding structure, functional groups, pyrolysis yield, crosslink density, molecular weight, or backbone architecture are reported. The paper is not relevant to preceramic polymer chemistry characterization.
source: Rishad_2025_Innovative fabrication pathways for ultra-high temperature ceramic matrix composites_progress, properties enhancements and future perspectives

elemental_composition.other_elements: Post-pyrolysis ceramic compositions given: SiCN = SiC0.95N0.85O0.1; SiCN-ZrO2 nanocomposite = SiZr0.13C0.5N0.8O0.7 (atomic ratios relative to Si, not atomic percent)

bonding_structure.other_bonds: Carbon described as aromatically bonded, possibly in form of a graphene network based on MD calculations and NMR data

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Polymer releases predominantly hydrogen (instead of hydrocarbons) upon pyrolysis, leaving excess carbon in the ceramic. Powders were annealed at 1300°C for 10 h in nitrogen atmosphere prior to characterization.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal, at low temperatures in flowing N2

backbone_architecture.description: Organic precursor crosslinked into a polymer with a glass transition temperature above the pyrolysis onset temperature; silazane used as SiCN source

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: SiCN contains amorphous nanodomains ~1.3 nm average size (SAXS). SiCN-ZrO2 nanocomposite contains tetragonal zirconia nanocrystals with average size ~4.3 nm (XRD), mean 3.6 nm and median 4.0 nm (SAXS), TEM range 3-6 nm. Zirconia volume fraction ~11 vol% in composite.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: PDCs noted for mechanical and chemical durability; SiCN exhibits extreme resistance to crystallization and high-temperature creep

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: SiCN: no diffraction peaks (amorphous). SiCN-ZrO2: tetragonal zirconia identified by Bragg diffraction and electron diffraction.

notes: Paper focuses on nanostructural characterization of polymer-derived SiCN ceramics using SAXS, Bragg diffraction, and TEM. Silazane precursor used with zirconium n-propoxide for nanocomposite. SiCN nanodomains (1.3 nm average, SAXS only) are amorphous and not detectable by XRD or TEM. ZrO2 crystallite size: ~4.3 nm (XRD Scherrer), mean 3.6 nm / median 4.0 nm (SAXS), 3-6 nm range (TEM). Annealing at 1300°C for 10 h in N2 prior to characterization. Grain size of 4.3 nm in notes field reflects XRD Scherrer result for zirconia; SAXS mean is 3.6 nm. PDI range note: size distribution of zirconia crystallites is asymmetric (mean < median).
source: Saha et al. - 2005 - Characterization of Nanodomains in Polymer‐Derived SiCN Ceramics Employing Multiple Techniques

elemental_composition.other_elements: Compositions vary across four samples (A-D): Sample A: SiO1.49C0.9, Sample B: SiO1.38C1.31, Sample C: SiO1C1.6, Sample D: SiO0.92C1.94

bonding_structure.other_bonds: sp2 carbon-carbon (graphitic/graphene network), sp3 carbidic Si-C bonds, mixed SiCnO4-n tetrahedral coordination, Si-O-Si bonds similar to silicates

functional_groups.other: Vinyl groups from tetravinylcyclotetrasiloxane precursor; Pt-catalyst used for crosslinking

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Polymer crosslinked at room temperature, aged 24h in Ar, heat treated at 400C for 5h in Ar, ball-milled, pyrolyzed at 1000C for 5h, then heat treated at 1200C for 1h in Ar. Hydrogen released in 700-900C range leaving excess carbon in ceramic.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: catalytic - Pt-catalyst (1 wt% of polymer) at room temperature

backbone_architecture.description: Highly crosslinked polymer or gel pyrolyzed into ceramic; precursor includes cyclic siloxane (1,3,5,7-tetramethyl-1,3,5,7-tetravinylcyclotetrasiloxane) mixed with linear PHMS; after pyrolysis forms cage-like graphene network encasing silica domain clusters

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Amorphous SiCO with nanodomains of silica clusters (1-5 nm) encased in mixed SiCO interfacial bonds and sp2 graphene network. No significant crystallization of SiC or silica (cristobalite) observed below decomposition temperatures. High-resolution TEM suggests graphitic carbon in nanoscale units and local SiC-like arrangements. SAXS reveals persistent nanodomains: Sample A ~2.3 nm, Sample B ~1.7 nm, Sample C ~1.1 nm, Sample D ~1.4 nm.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Exhibits viscoelastic behavior and high resistance to creep even at very high temperatures; no long-term steady-state creep observed

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: No significant crystallization of SiC or cristobalite (SiO2) detected by wide-angle XRD below decomposition temperatures

notes: Paper focuses on SiCO polymer-derived ceramics (PDCs), not a single polymer. Four SiCO compositions (A-D) prepared by varying ratio of PHMS to tetravinylcyclotetrasiloxane (5, 15, 50, 95 wt% vinyl precursor). Ceramic elemental analysis by combustion (C) and fusion (O) methods; Si calculated by difference. SAXS used to measure nanodomain size (1-5 nm); model predicts domain size decreases with increasing carbon content, consistent with Type B nanodomain model (silica clusters encased in mixed SiCO bonds and graphene network). Interdomain boundary widths predicted in range 760-1450 pm depending on composition and interface model parameter p. Si-O nearest neighbor bond at 162 pm, Si-C at 188-189 pm by radial distribution function. Carbon bonded to Si or itself but not to oxygen.
source: Saha et al. - 2006 - A Model for the Nanodomains in Polymer‐Derived SiCO

bonding_structure.other_bonds: Si-O-C mixed network confirmed by FTIR; C-O linkage absent in pyrolysed samples; vinyl groups from DVB react with Si-H via hydrosilylation

functional_groups.other: Divinylbenzene (DVB) used as crosslinker contributing aromatic carbon; Si-H confirmed absent in crosslinked green body after hydrosilylation reaction

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Ceramic yield ~71% at 1000°C and ~66% at 1400°C. Polymer to ceramic conversion complete at 1000°C; above this temperature mainly phase separation occurs. Heating and cooling rates of 50°C/h used. TGA data referenced from literature for PHMS/DVB composition.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: catalytic - platinum-catalyzed hydrosilylation using Karstedt's catalyst (Pt(0)-1,3-divinyl-1,1,3,3-tetramethyldisiloxane complex in xylene, ~2% Pt, ~700 ppm loading)

molecular_weight.measurement_method: Supplier specification (Sigma Aldrich) - MW ~1900 for PHMS

backbone_architecture.description: Crosslinked polysiloxane network formed by hydrosilylation reaction between polyhydromethylsiloxane (PHMS) and divinylbenzene (DVB) at a 1:2 weight ratio (PHMS:DVB). DVB acts as crosslinker introducing aromatic carbon bridges. Network gels within 30 min to 1 h.

microstructural.ceramic_phase: SiOC (amorphous at 1000°C); nanocrystalline SiC + amorphous SiO2-rich phase at 1400°C
microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Amorphous SiCxO2(1-x) phase plus ~50 wt% free carbon reported for PHMS/DVB derived ceramics. Phase separation into SiC and SiO2-rich phases begins above 1200°C due to carbothermal reduction. Nanocrystalline SiC (sphalerite structure) identified by XRD at 1300-1400°C. SiC whiskers observed on surface at 1400°C with ~100 nm average thickness and several micrometers in length.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Characteristic biaxial flexural strength (B3B method): 922 MPa with Weibull modulus m=7.4 at 1000°C; 295 MPa with m=2.5 at 1400°C. Reduced strength at 1400°C attributed to microcracks from carbothermal reduction and SiC whisker formation. Poisson's ratio assumed 0.22.

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: Amorphous SiOC at 800-1200°C; nanocrystalline SiC (sphalerite/cubic) appearing at 1300°C and sharper at 1400°C. XRD performed at Swiss Light Source Material Science Beamline, wavelength 0.56360 Å.

notes: DVB content is 2x by weight relative to PHMS to maximize free carbon content. Free carbon content reported ~50 wt% for this PHMS/DVB composition. Electrical conductivity increases from ~10^-7 S/cm at 800°C to ~10^1 S/cm at 1400°C, attributed to ordering of free carbon network (confirmed by Raman D/G band analysis). Raman spectra show D-band (~1350 cm-1) and G-band (~1600 cm-1) with increasing ID/IG ratio and decreasing FWHM at higher temperatures indicating carbon cluster growth and ordering. Ceramic yield range: 66-71% (midpoint 68.5 used); pyrolysis temperatures studied: 800, 900, 1000, 1100, 1200, 1300, 1400°C. Density: 1.52 g/cm3 at 1000°C, 1.62 g/cm3 at 1400°C. Volumetric shrinkage: 63% at 1000°C, 67% at 1400°C. Initial disc diameter 7 mm, final ~5.0 mm (1000°C) and ~4.7 mm (1400°C).
source: Sasikumar_2018_Polymer derived silicon oxycarbide ceramic monoliths_Microstructure development and associated materials properties

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: TGA measurements conducted on raw materials heated to 1000 C at 10 C/min in air or argon. Debindering step at 350 C with 1 h dwell; organic constituents pyrolyzed by 700 C to generate powderous green body. Heating from RT to 200 C at 5 C/min, then to 350 C at 1 C/min.

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: TiCx and Al2O3 impurities present; Ti3SiC2 phase stability dependent on carbon black content and sintering temperature. At 1600 C, Ti3SiC2 peak disappears at 8 wt% carbon black and TiC peak appears at 0 wt% carbon black.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Flexural strength (double-ring test) ranged from 13 MPa (uncalendered) to 83 MPa (calendered). Preceramic paper tensile strength: 0.25 MPa (2.4 um filler) to 1.75 MPa (14.8 um filler). Elongation before tearing: 0.4% (2.4 um) to 0.9% (14.8 um).

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: Ti3SiC2, TiCx, Al2O3

notes: This paper does not describe a preceramic polymer. It describes paper-derived Ti3SiC2 MAX-phase ceramics fabricated from preceramic papers filled with Ti3SiC2 particles, cellulose pulp fibers, and ionic starches. The organic components (cellulose, starch, polyacrylonitrile plasticizer, polyacrylamide retention aid) serve as binders/processing aids, not as preceramic polymers. Porosity ranged from 18.6 vol% (short fiber) to 45.3 vol% (long fiber); midpoint 31.95 vol% used above. Flexural strength midpoint 48 MPa used above (range 13-83 MPa). Ti3SiC2 filler particle size milled from 14.8 um to 2.4 um. Ceramic layers 300-700 um thick.
source: Schultheiß et al. - 2015 - Processing and characterization of paper-derived Ti3SiC2 based ceramic

bonding_structure.other_bonds: C-C bonds present in free carbon phase; sp2-C and sp3-C coordination described; C-O bonds observed in some models after aiMD

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Text notes that polymer-to-ceramic conversion is complete at about 1000 C; annealing between 1000-1200 C causes phase separation into amorphous SiO2, amorphous SiC, and free carbon; heat treatment at 1200 C and above yields SiC precipitates in amorphous silica with turbostratic graphitic carbon

backbone_architecture.description: Random network structure composed of Si-C and Si-O bonds resulting in a random distribution of SiCxO(4-x) tetrahedra; models range from random to segregated networks; glassy SiCO phase is stoichiometric with composition SiCxO(2-2x)

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Amorphous SiCO (SiCxO(2-2x)) glass with free carbon (sp2-C predominantly); phase separation at 1000-1200 C into amorphous SiO2, amorphous SiC, and free carbon; SiC precipitates embedded in amorphous silica at >1200 C; SiC segregation diameter 1-1.5 nm in models

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: No crystalline SiCO phase exists; crystalline references used are alpha-quartz SiO2 and beta-SiC; a-SiCO remains amorphous at temperatures where fused silica crystallizes

notes: This paper is a computational/theoretical study of amorphous silicon oxycarbide (a-SiCO) ceramics using DFT and ab initio molecular dynamics; it does not describe a preceramic polymer directly but rather the ceramic product derived from polymer pyrolysis. No polymer synthesis or characterization data are reported. Key findings: enthalpy of formation of glassy SiCO increases with increasing SiC content; segregated SiC/SiO2 models are lower in energy than random models; free carbon phase is predominantly sp2-C; interface between graphitic carbon and SiCO glass is unfavorable with interfacial energy ~0.8 J/m2; SiO2-rich surface minimizes surface tension at the glass-graphene interface. Models ranged from 128 to 793 atoms. Grain size range for SiC segregations was 1-1.5 nm (midpoint 1.25 nm used).
source: Searching insight into the atomistic structure of SiCO ceramics

polymer_name: Zr-PCS (transition-metal-crosslinked polycarbosilane; M-PCS designation used generally)

elemental_composition.other_elements: Zr, B, Cr, Hf, Mo, V, W, Nb present as crosslinkers or fillers; final ceramic composition reported as Zr-Si-O-C-B

bonding_structure.other_bonds: Si-CH2-Si (backbone linkage); C=C vinyl groups (terminal); O-H (trace moisture); Zr-Cl/Si-H dehydrochlorination crosslinks; Si-H and C=C consumed via hydrosilylation upon Zr crosslinking

functional_groups.other: Si-CH2-Si linkages in backbone; dehydrochlorination with metal chlorides (ZrCl4, HfCl4, CrCl3, VCl3)

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Weight loss reduced to ~7-10 wt% with ZrB2 filler incorporation. Pyrolysis via ultrafast electrical (Joule heating) method completed within 60 s at 1073 K in air. Without filler, Zr-PCS alone shows higher weight loss. Multiple phases (ZrB2, ZrO2, ZrC, SiC, C) identified post-pyrolysis. At 1673 K turbostratic carbon and SiC phases form.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal

backbone_architecture.description: Short-chain polycarbosilane (derived from polydimethylsilane via reflux) crosslinked with group IV-VI transition metal salts (ZrCl4, HfCl4, CrCl3, MoCl3, VCl3, etc.) via dehydrochlorination and hydrosilylation to form a tightly interlocked macromolecular network. Designed specifically as short-chain to enable uniform metal dispersion and lower decomposition temperatures compared to conventional long-chain PCPs.

microstructural.ceramic_phase: Zr-Si-O-C-B multiphase (ZrB2, ZrO2, ZrC, SiC, C)
microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Phases identified by XRD: ZrB2, ZrO2, ZrC, SiC, and C (graphitic/turbostratic carbon). ZrB2 nanoparticles retain crystalline cores encapsulated in graphitic carbon shell (core-shell structure). At higher temperatures (up to 1673 K), turbostratic carbon and additional SiC form. Dense, crack-free, nearly pore-free microstructure after electrical pyrolysis.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Adhesion testing per ASTM D3359 yielded 3B rating (moderate adhesion) on copper substrate. Thermal shock resistance demonstrated via oxygen-hydrogen torch test at >1423 K with no visible morphological changes.

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: ZrB2, ZrO2, ZrC, SiC, graphitic/turbostratic carbon

notes: Starting polymer is polydimethylsilane (PDM) converted to polycarbosilane (PCS) via reflux, then crosslinked with metal salts to form M-PCS. Primary system studied is Zr-PCS + ZrB2 filler (2:1 weight ratio, 0.6 wt% solvent). Additional transition metals explored as crosslinkers: Cr, Hf, Mo, V, W. Additional fillers explored: HfB2, TaC, NbC, TiB2. Ceramic yield >75% targeted with filler; ~90-93 wt% retained (7-10 wt% loss). Pyrolysis temperature of 1073 K cited as primary condition (800 C); range noted up to 1673 K for powder studies. Grain size range reported as 20-100 nm from TEM; midpoint 60 nm used. Electrical resistivity of ceramic-coated copper changes from 1.36e5 ohm·cm at 293 K to 2.61e5 ohm·cm at 1422 K. Oxidation resistance demonstrated at 1873 K for up to 30 min. d-spacings: d(102)=1.76 Å for graphene-like carbon, d(002)=3.54 Å for ZrB2. W-crosslinked ceramic showed ~5% average resistance change in oxidation stability tests.
source: Shenqiang Ren_2025_Compositionally complex ceramics from PCP

bonding_structure.other_bonds: Si-vinyl groups mentioned in context of photocurable moieties; B-N bonds implied in polyborosilazane/polyborazylene systems

functional_groups.other: methacryloyloxy groups (3-methacryloxypropyltrimethoxysilane); alkoxy groups (vinylmethoxysiloxane); photocurable moieties referenced generally

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Significant mass loss and gas evolution occur during pyrolysis; isotropic shrinkage of 20-30% typical; micro- to macro-scale porosity forms. Cyclic polymer structures yield higher ceramic yields than linear ones. SLA study reports ceramic yield increase from 36.9 to 38.4% with 0.5 wt% SiC filler. LOM study reports ceramic yield increased by 16 wt% with Si and SiC fillers. SLS study notes increasing laser energy results in decreased ceramic yield.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal, UV/photo (SLA/DLP/TPP), chemical (catalytic: zirconium acetylacetonate, tin-octoate, aluminium acetylacetonate, Dabco catalyst); crosslinkers can be dissolved in binder for spatial control in BJ

backbone_architecture.description: Silicon-based PCPs can have linear, cyclic, or branched architectures. Cyclic structures tend to produce higher ceramic yields than linear ones due to fewer volatile byproducts. Branched or non-linear structures are preferred to reduce loss of low molecular weight volatiles. Silsesquioxane (T-resin) structures implied for PMSQ.

microstructural.ceramic_phase: SiOC, SiCN, SiC, Si3N4, BN, SiCBN, borosilicate, wollastonite (CaSiO3), porous bioceramic, Zr-Si, composite ceramics
microstructural.phase_composition_notes: SiOC from polysiloxane pyrolysis; SiCN from polysilazane; SiC from polycarbosilane; BN from polyborazylene; SiCBN from polyborosilazane. Active fillers can produce carbides, nitrides, silicides in-situ. Mullite phase formed with Al2O3 filler. Wollastonite formed from PMSQ + CaCO3 reaction. Amorphous network formation noted for SiOC and SiCN.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Passive fillers reduce residual porosity to below 10 vol%; BJ-produced porous silicate bio-ceramics show low biaxial flexural strength. CNTs increase fracture toughness in SiCN at 1-2 mass% loading. MWCNTs increase tensile strength in SiCN fibers. Active fillers enhance hardness and thermal stability. Compressive strength enhanced by CaO/SrO/MgO/ZnO fillers in DIW.

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: SiOC (amorphous), SiCN (amorphous), SiC, Si3N4, mullite, wollastonite (CaSiO3), apatite, borosilicate phases noted

notes: This is a broad review paper covering multiple preceramic polymer types, additive manufacturing techniques, and ceramic systems. No single polymer is characterized in isolation with precise quantitative data for most fields. Key polymer systems discussed include: polysiloxanes (polymethylsiloxane, poly(methyl-silsesquioxane), poly(vinylmethoxysiloxane), methyl-phenyl-siloxane/methylsiloxane blends), polysilazanes, polycarbosilanes, polyborosilazanes, and polyborazylene. AM techniques covered: SLA, DLP, TPP, BJ, DIW, FDM, IJP, SLS/SLM, LOM. Shrinkage during pyrolysis is typically 20-30% isotropic. Active fillers can cause up to 50 vol% expansion compensating shrinkage. Passive fillers reduce porosity to below 10 vol%. UHTC-relevant phases highlighted: ZrB2, HfB2, ZrC, TaC. Ceramic yield values noted in specific AM studies: SLA with 0.5 wt% SiC increased yield from 36.9 to 38.4%; LOM with Si and SiC increased yield by 16 wt%. Typical powder size for BJ: 20-100 µm; BJ spherical feedstock particles: 45-90 µm. Pyrolysis atmosphere described as inert or reactive throughout.
source: Shenqiang Ren_2026_AM of Preceramic Polymers

notes: This paper is not about preceramic polymers. It is a study on spatially resolved electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) applied to conventional engineering thermoplastic polymer blends (PPS/PET, nylon 6/HDPE, PS/PE) for microstructural characterization. No preceramic polymer chemistry data are present in the text.
source: Siangchaew_1997_Energy-Loss Measurements of Polymer Microstructure and Polymer Interfaces_Issues and Opportunities

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: DTA-MS analysis performed; citric acid decomposes around 175 C; hydrogen emission observed around 500 C; nanostructured oxide forms at low temperatures and is reduced to MAX phase at high temperature

microstructural.ceramic_phase: Cr2GaC (MAX phase) with Cr3C2 side phase (~16 wt%)
microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Final product at 1050 C contains primarily Cr2GaC MAX phase with ~16 wt% Cr3C2 impurity; nanostructured disordered graphite also present; intermediate phases include nanostructured mixed Cr/Ga oxide resembling spinel with tetrahedral and octahedral coordination, and crystalline Cr2O3 at 800 C

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: Cr2GaC (MAX phase, P63mmc), Cr3C2; intermediate: nanostructured mixed oxide (spinel-like), Cr2O3

notes: This paper is NOT about preceramic polymers. It concerns sol-gel synthesis of the MAX phase Cr2GaC (a ternary layered carbide) from metal nitrates (Cr-nitrate, Ga-nitrate) and citric acid as carbon source in water. No preceramic polymer is involved. Refined unit cell parameters for Cr2GaC: a = 2.89129(3) Å, c = 12.6090(2) Å. The nanostructured oxide intermediate at 725 C refines to a crystallite diameter of ~17 Å. The disordered graphite nanostructure at 1050 C has a spherical crystallite size of ~8 Å. All JSON fields related to preceramic polymer chemistry are null as the paper does not describe such a material.
source: Siebert et al. - 2022 - Towards a mechanistic understanding of the sol–gel syntheses of ternary carbides

bonding_structure.other_bonds: Si-OH (residual hydroxyl from incomplete condensation); bridging Si-O-Si in ring structures

functional_groups.other: ethoxy groups (OEt) present in monomer MTES, converted to bridging oxygen during hydrolysis-condensation; residual OH groups from incomplete condensation

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Two distinct pyrolysis regimes identified: low-temperature regime A (550-700°C) dominated by evolution of silane and disiloxane fragments (M/z=73, M/z=147) and minor methane; high-temperature regime B (700-850°C) dominated by methane and hydrogen evolution with minor ethylene and water. Integrated weight loss: 2.85±0.35% for peak A, 10.1±0.8% for peak B. CHR experiments conducted at 2, 5, 10, 20, and 50°C/min; isothermal experiments at 647°C and 734°C for 60 min. Samples pre-treated at 530°C for 30 min before data collection. First-order reaction kinetics confirmed by Lorentzian peak fits and isothermal exponential decay.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal (sol-gel condensation with ammonia catalyst; cross-linked polymer formed prior to pyrolysis)

backbone_architecture.description: Three-dimensional molecular network derived from hydrolysis-condensation of methyltriethoxysilane (MTES); conceptual schematic shows rings of silicon and oxygen bonded via oxygen atoms with methyl groups on each silicon; occasional residual OH groups

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Ceramic composition written as 0.24SiC:0.76SiO2:0.44C (point F); ideal starting composition would be 0.25SiC:0.75SiO2:0.75C (point S, if only H removed). SiC:SiO2 ratio nearly unchanged during pyrolysis (n from 0.25 to 0.24). Less than 2.5% of Si atoms removed as volatile silanes; less than half of carbon atoms lost as methane. Free carbon present as excess carbon relative to stoichiometric SiC/SiO2 mixture.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Creep rates in PDC nanostructured materials noted to be extremely slow; carbon restricts mobility of molecular species

notes: Polymer derived from methyltriethoxysilane (MTES) via sol-gel hydrolysis-condensation (H2O/OEt=1, pH 1 HCl, reflux 70°C 10 min, then NH3/MTES=1/5 as condensation promoter). Gelled within 12 h, dried at RT 1 week then 60°C 1 week. Cylindrical samples 6mm x 25mm, crushed to ~30 µm powder for TGA. TGA conducted with Netzsch STA 409 in Ar at 100 mL/min. TG/MS used Leybold Hereaus Quadrex 200 quadrupole MS. Chemical analysis of ceramic performed by Service d'Analyze Elementaire du CNRS, France. Low-temperature peak A may represent two overlapping first-order reactions (silane M/z=73 and disiloxane M/z=147 evolution). High-temperature peak B well-described by single Lorentzian (methane + hydrogen evolution). Activation energies discussed but specific values not extracted from provided text sections.
source: Soraru_2002_Pyrolysis Kinetics for the Conversion of a Polymer into an Amorphous Silicon Oxycarbide Ceramic

polymer_name: POSS-based enaminone vitrimer (POSS1 and POSS2 series)

bonding_structure.other_bonds: Si-O-Si (POSS cage backbone at ~1075 cm-1); enaminone C=C (~1600 cm-1) and N-H bending (~1650 cm-1); beta-ketoester C=O (~1725 cm-1) present in precursors, absent after crosslinking

functional_groups.other: beta-ketoester groups on POSS cage; enaminone crosslinks formed upon reaction with diamines; hydroxyl groups on intermediate POSS derivatives

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Char yields at 650 C under N2: X1=41%, H1=35%, D1=28%, X2=51%, H2=43%, D2=38%. No appreciable change in char yield observed from 650 C to 1150 C. POSS1 vitrimers show two distinct decomposition modes; three distinct exotherms observed in DSC at ~300 C (POSS core cracking), ~450 C (carbonization of organic component), and ~600-700 C (crystallization to carbonaceous amorphous glass). POSS2 vitrimers show increased Td and char yields vs POSS1 counterparts. Shape retention of char observed after pyrolysis. Atmospheric stability tests conducted at 300, 650, and 1100 C in air at 10 C/min with 12 h hold.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: chemical - step-growth polycondensation/transamination of beta-ketoester-functionalized POSS with diamines; thermal curing at 85 C under vacuum for 6 h; compression molding at 160 C

notes: This is a broad review article on polymer-derived ceramics (PDCs) focusing on the fate and role of in situ formed free carbon. It does not report a single polymer with defined properties but rather surveys many preceramic polymer classes (polycarbosilanes, polysiloxanes, polysilazanes, poly(silylcarbodiimides), polyborosilazanes) and their derived ceramics. Specific polymer designations mentioned include KiON HTT1800, Perhydropolysilazane, ABSE polysilazane/polycarbosilazane, Polyhydridomethylsiloxane, Polyhydromethylsiloxane, Polymethoxymethylsiloxane, Allylhydridopolycarbosilane, Polycarbosilane (PCS), Polyvinylsilane, Polysiloxane mixed with BSAS. Coating applications on stainless steel and other substrates at pyrolysis temperatures 600-1350 degrees C are described. Electrochemical (Li-ion battery anode), electromagnetic absorption/shielding, thermal, and mechanical properties of derived ceramics are tabulated. Free carbon morphology and content are controlled by polymer molecular design (R group saturation/unsaturation) and thermal treatment conditions.

Polysilazane-derived SiCN crystallizes at temperatures 50-100 C lower than polysilylcarbodiimide-derived SiCN with analogous C/Si ratio. Supercapacitor performance data for SiOC and SiCN materials included in table.

notes: This paper is a review of wood-derived carbide processing techniques and is not primarily focused on preceramic polymer characterization. The polymer precursor infiltration (PPI) section references polycarbosilane (PCS) and polyzirconobutanediol (PZC) as the main preceramic polymers. PCS is used to produce SiC; PZC ([Zr(acac)2O2C4H8]n) is used to produce ZrC. The PPI technique involves infiltrating these precursors into wood-derived biocarbon scaffolds followed by pyrolysis. Key challenge noted is poor wettability between carbon scaffold and precursors, and volume contraction/cracking during pyrolysis. Compressive strength of 60 MPa was the highest achieved for the C-SiC-ZrC composite. notes: This is a broad review paper covering multiple preceramic polymer families and additive manufacturing techniques for polymer-derived ceramics. No single polymer system is characterized in detail; quantitative values for elemental composition, molecular weight, crosslink density, and most thermal pyrolysis parameters are not reported for individual polymers. Shrinkage during pyrolysis is generally 20-30% (isotropic). Active fillers can cause volumetric expansion of up to 50 vol% compensating for shrinkage. SiC filler addition in SLA reduced shrinkage from 43.1 to 37.2% and increased ceramic yield from 36.9 to 38.4%. LOM with Si and SiC fillers increased ceramic yield by 16 wt% and reduced shrinkage by 17%. IJP with polycarbosilane binder and SiC filler resulted in reduced volumetric shrinkage of 8.2% with no cracks. SPS heating rates noted as 10^2 to 10^3 °C/min. Flash sintering timescale 0.1-60 s.

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Pyrolysis results in significant mass loss and gas evolution, typically accompanied by isotropic shrinkage of 20-30% and formation of micro- to macro-scale porosity. Increasing laser energy in SLS results in decreased ceramic yield. SiC filler addition to SLA-processed poly(vinylmethoxysiloxane) increased ceramic yield from 36.9 to 38.4% while reducing shrinkage from 43.1 to 37.2%. LOM with Si and SiC fillers increased ceramic yield by 16 wt% and reduced shrinkage by 17%.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal, UV/photo (light-curable), chemical; catalysts include zirconium acetylacetonate (ZrAcAc), tin-octoate (TinOc), aluminium-acetylacetonate, Dabco

backbone_architecture.description: Silicon-based PCPs can have linear, cyclic, or branched architectures. Cyclic structures tend to produce higher ceramic yields than linear ones, as linear structures release more volatile byproducts during pyrolysis. Branched or non-linear molecular structures are preferred to reduce loss of low molecular weight volatiles.

microstructural.ceramic_phase: SiC, Si3N4, SiCN, SiOC, SiCBN, BN, borosilicate
microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Polysilanes yield SiC; polycarbosilanes yield SiC; polysilazanes yield Si3N4 and SiCN; poly(organosilylcarbodiimides) yield SiCN; polysiloxanes yield SiOC; polyborosilazane/polyborosilane/polyborosiloxane yield SiCBN or borosilicate ceramics; polyborazylene yields BN. Active fillers can lead to in-situ formation of carbides, nitrides, or silicides. Volumetric expansion of active fillers up to 50 vol% compensates for shrinkage.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Passive fillers reduce residual porosity to below 10 vol%, improving mechanical integrity. CNT addition to SiCN increases fracture toughness substantially at 1-2 mass% CNT concentration. MWCNTs increase tensile strength of SiCN-based fibers. BJ-fabricated bio-ceramic scaffolds exhibited low biaxial flexural strength.

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: Amorphous network formation noted for SiOC and SiCN during pyrolysis; crystalline phases such as mullite form upon addition of Al2O3 fillers; wollastonite (CaSiO3) forms from PMSQ with CaCO3

notes: This is a broad review paper covering multiple preceramic polymer families and additive manufacturing techniques for polymer-derived ceramics. No single polymer system is characterized in detail; specific quantitative compositional or thermal data for individual polymers are largely absent. Key polymer systems discussed include poly(methyl-silsesquioxane) (PMSQ), polymethylsiloxane (PMS), poly(vinylmethoxysiloxane), methyl-phenyl-siloxane/methylsiloxane blends, polycarbosilane, and 3-methacryloxypropyltri-methoxysilane. AM techniques covered: SLA, DLP, TPP, BJ, DIW, FDM, IJP, SLS/SLM, LOM. Shrinkage during pyrolysis typically 20-30% isotropically. Active fillers can cause up to 50 vol% expansion to compensate shrinkage. UHTC-relevant compositions highlighted include ZrB2, HfB2, ZrC, TaC. Spark plasma sintering heating rates cited as 100-1000 °C/min.
source: Additive manufacturing pathways for polymer-derived ceramics_ processing, structure, and function

notes: This paper is a review of inkjet printing as an additive manufacturing technique for ceramic components. It contains no preceramic polymer chemistry data. The text covers drop generation mechanisms (CIJ, DOD, EIJ), ink rheological requirements, drop impact physics, and process conditions. No polymer type, elemental composition, bonding structure, pyrolysis data, or any other preceramic polymer descriptors are present in the provided text.
source: Additive_Manufacture_of_Ceramics_Components_by_Ink

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Polymer-to-ceramic conversion occurs with gas release and shrinkage at 400-800 degrees C. A SiOC coffee cup was pyrolyzed at 1200 degrees C. A SiOC diamond structure was pyrolyzed at 1000 degrees C.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal/catalytic - catalyst mixed into printing liquid enables cross-linking in successive heat treatment; two printing heads can print some areas with catalyst and others without

backbone_architecture.description: Text notes that composition, molecular architecture, and molecular weight can be modified to adapt preceramic polymers to specific additive manufacturing processing requirements, but no specific architectural details are given.

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Polysiloxanes yield SiOC, polysilazanes yield SiCN, polycarbosilanes yield SiC after pyrolysis. When heat-treated in air, polysiloxane leaves a SiO2 residue that can react with inorganic fillers to provide silicate ceramic phases. Apatite-wollastonite bioglass-ceramic scaffolds also mentioned. SiSiC lattice structures produced by infiltration with liquid silicon.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Text mentions enhanced mechanical characteristics as a goal of further development but provides no specific measured values.

notes: This paper is a review/overview article on additive manufacturing of preceramic polymers. It does not report detailed characterization data for a specific polymer. Key points: (1) Preceramic polymers discussed include polysiloxanes, polysilazanes, polycarbosilanes, polyborosilazanes, and borazine-based systems. (2) Polysiloxane powders noted as commercially available at low cost in large amounts; polysilazanes also commercially available at low-medium cost; polycarbosilanes have limited availability and high cost; boron-containing polymers require custom synthesis and are very expensive. (3) Printed polysiloxane powder bed relative density ~45%, printed part relative density ~80%. (4) Additive manufacturing techniques discussed: powder 3D printing (100 µm resolution), inkjet printing (20 µm), laminated object manufacturing (100 µm), direct ink writing (60 µm), fused deposition modeling (100 µm), stereolithography (25 µm), two-photon photopolymerization (<1 µm). (5) Preceramic polymers can be mixed with reactive or inert fillers. (6) Direct ink writing inks require non-Newtonian, shear-thinning behavior with yield stress; nozzle diameter 60 µm to 2 mm.
source: Additive_Manufacturing_techniques_for_fa

elemental_composition.other_elements: B mentioned in borosilazane systems; Ti, Al, Zr mentioned as additional elements possible

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Weight loss of typically 10-30 wt.-% associated with organic-inorganic transition almost terminated at 800-1000 C. Ceramic yield reported up to more than 90 wt.-% for novel precursors. Table 1 references ceramic yields: hydridosilazane 0.74, hydridomethylsilazane 0.72-0.85, vinylsilazane 0.85, vinylphenylsilazane 0.85, cyclomethylsilazane 0.88, borosilazane 0.9 and 0.72 and 0.7 depending on system. Open-pore channel network forms above 400 C, diminishes at 800-1000 C (transient porosity). Density increases by factor 2-3 from precursor (~1 g/cm3) to ceramic residue.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal annealing at 100-250 C in oxidative atmosphere; chlorosilane cross-linking; microwave, electron or gamma-ray radiation curing

backbone_architecture.description: General formula with tetravalent silicon and bridging units X = O (polysiloxane), NH (polysilazane), CH2 (polycarbosilane); R, R' = H, alkyl, aryl, arenyl; amorphous covalent network formed upon pyrolysis; borosilazanes contain B in backbone

microstructural.ceramic_phase: SiC, Si3N4, SiOC, SiCN, SiBNC, BN, SiO2, B4C
microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Crystalline phases precipitate at different temperatures depending on composition: 800-1000 C for SiC-based systems, >1600 C for Si-BN-C. Excessive carbon present as carbon clusters (BSU) at lower temperatures and graphitic carbon ribbons at higher temperatures. Nicalon SiC fiber contains beta-SiC crystals and C-precipitations in amorphous SiOC matrix. Boron shifts crystallization temperature up to 1600 C. H below 1000 C suppresses devitrification.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: MOR0 estimated at 650 MPa at zero porosity for filler-containing poly(siloxane)-derived Si-O-C ceramics (Ryskewitch expression with b=5 for spherical pores). Matrix fracture toughness KI0 of amorphous pyrolysis products < 2 MPa*m^0.5. Creep rate of 10^-7 s^-1 at 1500 C under 100 MPa constant load for poly(siloxane)/MoSi2 pyrolyzed in nitrogen, comparable to hot-pressed Si3N4 and SiC.

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: SiC (beta), Si3N4, SiO2, BN, B4C identified as possible crystalline precipitates upon heating; Si3N4/SiC, SiC/N, Si3N4, SiBN3C, BN/Si3N4 referenced in table

notes: This is a review paper covering multiple preceramic polymer systems (polysilazane, polycarbosilane, polysiloxane, polyborosilazane) rather than a single polymer study. Ceramic yields from Table 1 (as weight fractions): hydridosilazane pyrolyzed at 1200 C/N2 = 0.74; hydridomethylsilazane pyrolyzed at 1000 C/Ar = 0.72 and methylsilazane = 0.85; vinylsilazane at 800 C/NH3 and 1200 C/N2 = 0.85; vinylphenylsilazane at 1000 C/N2 = 0.85; cyclomethylsilazane at 1000 C/Ar = 0.88; borosilazane at 1000 C/Ar = 0.9, borosiliciumimide at 1250 C/N2 = 0.72; borosilazane at 1650 C/Ar = 0.7. Reactive fillers (Ti, Cr, V, Si, B, CrSi2, MoSi2, AlN, etc.) used to compensate pyrolysis shrinkage; filler volume fractions of 0.15-0.3 needed for net-shape processing. MoSi2-containing Si-O-C composites show electrical conductivity ~10^4 S/m and oxidation stability >1400 C. Percolation threshold for insulator-conductor transition in MoSi2-loaded SiOC is V_f = 0.2-0.3. SiC from poly(carbosilane) forms at 800-1500 C vs 1900-2200 C for sintering. Fiber systems discussed: Nicalon (SiC/SiOC), Tyranno (SiC+TiC), Si3N4/SiNxOy, Si-B-N-C stable to 1500 C.
source: Adv Eng Mater - 2000 - Greil - Polymer Derived Engineering Ceramics

bonding_structure.other_bonds: Si-vinyl (C2H3) groups present in H62C; Si-phenyl (C6H5) groups present in H62C; Si-OCH3 and Si-OC2H5 groups present in MTMS and MTES respectively; hydrosilylation between vinyl and Si-H groups in H62C

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Pyrolysis temperatures range from 1200 to 1600C. Temperatures below 1400C result in total porosity less than 2%. Above 1400C, accelerated SiO gas formation increases porosity. Polymer-to-ceramic conversion yields Si-C-O ceramic material. Density increases from ~1 to ~3 g/cm3 during conversion. Ceramic yield stated as up to 90 wt% at moderate pyrolysis temperatures of 1000-1600C. Hold times range from 4 to 16 hours at peak temperature.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal/chemical - condensation reaction of methoxy, ethoxy and hydroxy groups catalyzed by oleic acid (<100C) and aluminum acetylacetonate (>100C); hydrosilylation of vinyl and Si-H groups in H62C; stepwise heating to 60C, 90C, and 130C maximum

backbone_architecture.description: Organopolysilsesquioxanes [RSiO1.5]n with R = -CH3, -C6H5, -C2H3, -C3H7, -H; cross-linking active between 100-300C forming a network structure via condensation of alkoxy/hydroxy groups and hydrosilylation

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Pyrolysis in argon yields Si-O-C ceramic matrix with SiC and free carbon. Pyrolysis in nitrogen at temperatures >1400C yields SiC-Si2ON2 composite ceramic. Formation of Si2ON2 from reaction of SiO gas with nitrogen results in 11.5% specific volume increase relative to initial Si volume. At 1550-1600C in nitrogen, complete conversion to SiC-Si2ON2 composite reported.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Flexural strength (ring-on-ring, DIN 52291): 67 ± 13 MPa for samples pyrolyzed in argon at ~32% porosity and 0.25 µm pore size; 115 ± 14 MPa for 30SiC-10Si samples pyrolyzed in nitrogen at 1550C with 29 vol% porosity and 0.14 µm median pore size

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: SiC, Si2ON2 identified by XRD with monochromated Cu Kα radiation

notes: Paper describes fabrication of ceramic tapes by doctor blade process using polysiloxane slurries (organopolysilsesquioxanes) loaded with Si and SiC reactive fillers. Two slurry compositions used: 30Si-10SiC and 30SiC-10Si (vol%). Catalysts: 0.5 vol% oleic acid and 0.5 vol% Al(acac)3. Slurry also contains MTES (18 vol%) as reactive silane monomer. Free carbon detected by Raman spectroscopy (D and G bands at 514 nm excitation). Nitrogen content measured by Leco TC 136 analyzer. Porosity measured by Hg intrusion porosimetry. Thermodynamic calculations (HSC Chemistry 4.1) predict decomposition of Si2ON2 and SiC above 1800-1900C. The ceramic system is described as Si-O-C-(N). Porosity data from Table 2 ranges from 1.6% to 45% depending on filler ratio, pyrolysis temperature and atmosphere.
source: Adv Eng Mater - 2002 - Cromme - Ceramic Tapes from Preceramic Polymers

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: TGA oxidation experiments performed at 1200, 1300, and 1400 °C in synthetic air with 5 K/min heating rate and 5 h dwell times. Parabolic weight gain behavior observed. Weight gain at 1300 °C after 10 h oxidation ~1.84 wt% for SiHfBCN2 powder.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal

backbone_architecture.description: HTT1800 is a commercially available polysilazane; backbone architecture not described in this text

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: All powder and monolithic SiHfBCN samples confirmed amorphous by XRD prior to oxidation. After oxidation at temperatures below 1300 °C, oxide scale consists of borosilicate, silica, m- and t-HfO2. Above 1300 °C, oxide scale consists of silica, HfSiO4, m- and t-HfO2 and becomes discontinuous due to boria evaporation.

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: Amorphous for all as-pyrolyzed samples; post-oxidation phases include borosilicate, silica, m-HfO2, t-HfO2, HfSiO4

notes: Paper focuses on high-temperature oxidation behavior of polymer-derived SiHfBCN ceramics (powders and monoliths) at 1200-1400 °C. HTT1800 polysilazane was modified with Hf(N(Et)2)4 at volume ratios of 90:10 (SiHfBCN1) and 70:30 (SiHfBCN2) relative to the polysilazane, and with BH3·SMe2 at a Hf(NEt2)4:BH3·SMe2 molar ratio of 1:2. Cross-linking performed at 200-250 °C for 3 h in argon. Pyrolysis at 1100 °C in purified argon; monoliths additionally annealed at 1300 °C. Open porosity of monoliths: 5.8 vol% (SiHfBCN1) and 10.4 vol% (SiHfBCN2). Specific surface area: 4.71 m2/g (SiHfBCN2 powder), 3.26 m2/g (SiHfBCN1 monolith), 3.34 m2/g (SiHfBCN2 monolith). Corrected parabolic oxidation rates (10^-9 to 10^-8 mg2 cm^-4 h^-1) indicate excellent oxidation resistance. Activation energy for SiHfBCN2 powder: 112.9 kJ/mol; for SiHfBCN1 monolith: 174 ± 58 kJ/mol; for SiHfBCN2 monolith: 140 ± 39 kJ/mol.
source: Adv Eng Mater - 2014 - Fabrizi - In Situ Reinforcement of Ti6Al4V Matrix Composites by Polymer‐Derived‐Ceramics Phases

polymer_name: PCS Type S, Nippon Carbon Co. Ltd

elemental_composition.other_elements: C/Si molar ratio after pyrolysis in Ar is nearly 2:1; C/SiC ratio in pyrolytic product is 1:1

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Pyrolysis of PCS releases active free-carbon and silicon species that promote formation of TiC and Ti3SiC2 phases when mixed with TiH2. Temperatures tested ranged from 1000 to 1600 C with dwell times up to 5 h. Optimal conditions were 1400 C for 5 h. Above 1400 C, Si sublimation leads to prevalence of TiC and disappearance of Ti3SiC2.

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: At optimized conditions (1400 C, 5 h, 20% excess PCS): 73 wt% Ti3SiC2, 21 wt% TiC, 6 wt% Ti5Si3. In Ti/Ti3SiC2 composite (70/30 wt/wt target): semi-quantitative XRD gave 72 wt% Ti, 16 wt% TiC, 12 wt% Ti3SiC2. Some residual porosity observed.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Ti/Ti3SiC2/TiC composites showed greatly increased wear resistance and increased hardness compared to pure Ti. Friction coefficient and worn volume were lower for the composite than for pure Ti under identical test conditions.

notes: PCS is used as a reactive preceramic filler mixed with TiH2 powder to synthesize Ti3SiC2 (MAX phase) and TiC in situ upon pyrolysis in Ar. The paper focuses on colloidal processing and direct foaming using PCS/TiH2 emulsions with methylcellulose for viscosity control. PCS dissolved in hexane (6.36 g PCS in 41.71 ml hexane) was used. 4 wt% CaF2 added as sintering aid. Foams targeted Ti/Ti3SiC2 ratio of 70/30 wt/wt. Porosity up to 85 vol% reported for PCS-derived foams at 1000 C from prior literature cited in the paper. Hold time range 2-5 h; midpoint ~3.5 h used for notes but 300 min (5 h) used as the optimized hold time in pyrolysis_temp field.
source: Adv Eng Mater - 2017 - Molero - Ti Ti3SiC2  TiC  Bulk and Foam Composites by Pyrolysis of Polycarbosilane and TiH2 Mixtures

notes: This is a review paper covering 30 years of Si-B-C-N polymer-derived ceramics research. No single specific polymer with quantified properties is described; data extracted reflects general trends and early precursor systems discussed (Takamizawa et al., Seyferth et al.). Precursors include blends/copolymers of polysilane+organoboron compounds and single-source precursors. Amorphous ceramics obtained at 800-1000°C; crystallization of Si-C-N around 1400°C; Si-B-C-N stable up to 2000°C. Chlorosilanes (SiRxCl4-x) are primary molecular building blocks. RF-cured samples (3 wt% MWCNT) showed ~95% cure extent vs 100% for convective oven. 3D printed multilayer structures showed ~97% cure extent. RF-cured fibers showed ~96% cure extent. Microwave pyrolysis at 800 W for 60 s used to directly pyrolyze fibers.

XPS also confirms SiC as major surface phase. Polycarbosilane forms amorphous SiC at 850 C and crystalline SiC after sintering above 1200-1300 C.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Storage modulus and loss modulus of 3D printing ink described; crossover (flow point) at ~35 Pa shear stress; ink exhibits shear thinning behavior from 0.01 to 100 1/s

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: beta-SiC (cubic lattice)

notes: Study focuses on MWCNT-loaded polycarbosilane composites (1-6 wt% MWCNT) processed via microwave and RF heating as oven-free/mold-free routes to SiC. Pyrolysis temperatures cited: crosslinking/curing at ~400 C, amorphous SiC formation at ~850 C, dense crystalline SiC sintering above 1200-1300 C. RF resonance achieved at ~76-78 MHz; 3D printing ink cured at 100 MHz. Ink composition: polycarbosilane + one-part catalyst (65 wt%), MWCNT (6 wt%), SiC nanoparticles (29 wt%). Polycarbosilane melting point ~90 C. SiC fibers extruded with 6 wt% MWCNT and RF-cured at 100 W, ~50 s, 98 MHz. Beta-SiC described as having more surface area and superior electrical and thermal properties versus other SiC phases.

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: TGA/DSC performed on cylindrical green body sample to 800 °C at 5 °C/min to characterize binder burnout. Debinding cycle designed based on results, spanning ambient to ~600 °C over ~48 h with multiple isothermal holds. Sintering performed at 1625 °C with 2 h dwell in air. This is not a preceramic polymer pyrolysis process; the ceramic material is alpha-Al2O3 processed via DLP with photopolymer binder.

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Alumina cellular structures sintered at 1625 °C; dielectric constant of bulk alumina reported as 9 to 10, with simulation value of 9.6 used; effective dielectric constant varies with porosity of cellular structure

notes: This paper does not describe a preceramic polymer. It describes the fabrication of cellular alumina (Al2O3) structures via digital light processing (DLP) additive manufacturing using a photocurable ceramic slurry for antenna waveguide dielectric applications. The slurry contains alpha-Al2O3 powders (SA8MAR, Baikowski), difunctional monomer HDDA, tetrafunctional monomer EBECRYL 892, photoinitiator Omnirad 819, dispersant DisperBYK-111, poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate diluent, and a yellow dye light absorber. Thermal processing involves debinding to ~600 °C and sintering at 1625 °C in air. The focus is on tuning effective dielectric constant (range ~4.86 to 7.5 achieved) via porosity variation in cubic lattice structures for waveguide antenna cutoff frequency reduction (target 1-10 GHz range). None of the preceramic polymer descriptors are applicable to this work.
source: Adv Eng Mater - 2024 - Rosa - Design  Additive Manufacturing  and Electromagnetic Characterization of Alumina Cellular

notes: This paper is a NASA Ames Research Center overview presentation on ceramic matrix composites and thermal protection systems (TPS) for aerospace vehicles. It does not contain preceramic polymer chemistry data. The text mentions polymer precursors and ceramic coating processing only in passing, with no quantitative or structural polymer data provided. Materials discussed are primarily ZrB2/SiC and HfB2/SiC composites for hypersonic TPS applications.
source: Advanced Ceramic Matrix Composites for TPS

polymer_name: MK, H44, H62C (silicones from Wacker Chemie AG); PSZ20 (KiON Defence Technologies); NN120-20 (Clariant AG)

bonding_structure.other_bonds: Si-based backbone containing C, O, N, B, and H atoms described generally for organo-silicon preceramic polymers

thermal_pyrolysis.pyrolysis_atmosphere: nitrogen or argon (inert); air for silicate production
thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: MK silicone polymer yields ~84% of starting weight converted into silica when fired in air. Pyrolysis typically above 800 C in non-oxidative atmosphere. Decomposition gases include methane, benzene, and hydrogen. Density increases from ~0.8-1.2 g/cm3 (polymer) to ~2.2 g/cm3 (amorphous Si-based ceramic). Amorphous SiCO and SiCN residues begin carbothermal decomposition above ~1250 C. Polysilazane curing at 350 C for 1 h under flowing N2.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal (curing at 350 C for 1 h under flowing N2 mentioned for polysilazanes); chemical/catalytic crosslinking mentioned generally

backbone_architecture.description: Organo-silicon polymers with Si-O backbone (silicones/polysiloxanes) or Si-N backbone (polysilazanes); polymer chains bear -OH side groups enabling condensation reactions with metal alkoxides

microstructural.ceramic_phase: SiOC (silicon oxycarbide) from silicones in inert atmosphere; SiO2 (amorphous silica) from silicones in air; SiCN (silicon carbonitride) from polysilazanes; silicates (mullite, wollastonite, zircon, etc.) and SiAlONs when nano-sized active fillers are used
microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Amorphous SiCO contains nano-sized SiC domains and free carbon clusters. SiCN contains nano-sized N- and C-rich areas at low pyrolysis temperature, developing Si3N4 and SiC nano-regions above ~1250 C. SiAlOC residue stable up to 1300 C; yields nano-crystalline mullite and SiC above 1300 C. ZrO2 nano-particles form agglomerates not exceeding critical size for tetragonal-to-monoclinic transformation.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Fracture toughness KC ~6.5 MPa·m0.5 for ZTM (zirconia toughened mullite) composites. Addition of 1-2 wt% MWCNTs increases fracture toughness via pull-out and bridging. Young modulus and Poisson's ratio unaffected by up to 2 wt% MWCNTs. Graphene nano-platelets in polycarbosilane-derived SiC increase strength and microhardness.

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: Mullite (3Al2O3·2SiO2), ZrO2 (tetragonal, ~5 nm at 1300 C), hafnia (tetragonal HfO2), Si3N4, SiC, Fe3Si, Fe5Si3, zircon (ZrSiO4), hafnon (HfSiO4), SiAlON phases (beta-prime, Ca-alpha-prime), yttrium silicates (Y2O3·SiO2, Y2O3·2SiO2), wollastonite, cordierite, gehlenite, akermanite, hardystonite, willemite

notes: This is a review paper covering multiple preceramic polymer systems (polysiloxanes/silicones and polysilazanes primarily, with some polycarbosilane references) and their modification with nano-sized active fillers, passive fillers (CNTs, graphene), and chemical additives (metal alkoxides). Key polymers identified: MK, H44, H62C (silicones, Wacker Chemie AG); PSZ20 (KiON polysilazane); NN120-20 (Clariant polysilazane). Ceramic yield of 84% is specifically for MK silicone polymer converted to silica in air. Grain size <300 nm refers to mullite monoliths. Porosity below 15 vol% refers to crack-free monoliths from Greil's approach. Hafnia nano-crystal diameter of 5 nm at 1300 C. Crystallite size of 5 nm refers specifically to tetragonal hafnia. notes: This paper focuses on Ti-, Zr-, Hf-, and TiZrHf-based preceramic polymers synthesized via copper(I)-catalyzed azide-alkyne (CuAAC) click chemistry - NOT silicon-based PCPs. The polymers contain no Si. Metals incorporated as metallocene units (cyclopentadienyl complexes). Polymer synthesis: metallocene diazides prepared from tributylstannyl-azide + dichloro metallocene, then click-polymerized with 1,4-diethynylbenzene. Polymers are insoluble powders. Structural evolution characterized using synchrotron HE-XRD, atomic PDF analysis, Reverse Monte Carlo (RMC) simulations, XAS (Ti K-edge, Zr L3-edge XANES and EXAFS), Raman spectroscopy, and HAADF-STEM/EDS. Conversion mechanism: polymer -> metal oxide + amorphous carbon (800-1100 C) -> metal carbide via carbothermal reduction (1500 C). RMC-derived coordination numbers for TiC at 1500 C: Ti-C CN=5.9 (bulk=6), Ti-Ti CN=11.8 (bulk=12). ZrC at 1500 C: Zr-C CN=5.5 (bulk=6), Zr-Zr CN=10.5 (bulk=12). HfC at 1500 C: CN values approach bulk. Excess carbon noted in all systems, attributed to polymeric precursor stoichiometry. Hf-based system shows more excess carbon than Zr-based. Paper does not report ceramic yield %, molecular weight, heating rate, or hold time explicitly.
source: Atomic‐scale structure elucidation of refractory metal carbides derived from metallocene‐based preceramics

notes: This paper is not about preceramic polymers. It concerns the fabrication of aluminum nitride (AlN) ceramic components via binder jetting (BJ) additive manufacturing followed by sintering and hot isostatic pressing (HIPing). No preceramic polymer is described. The binder used in BJ is not chemically characterized in the text. Sintering was performed at 1500 °C (ramp rate 5 °C/min, dwells at 150 °C for 1 h, 600 °C for 20 min, 1500 °C for 5 h) in argon atmosphere with vacuum purge. Thermal conductivity of HIPed AlN measured 4.82 W/m·K at 23 °C and 3.17 W/m·K at 500 °C; sintered-only pellet showed 2.8 W/m·K at room temperature and 1.4 W/m·K at 500 °C. notes: This paper is NOT about preceramic polymers. It concerns binder jet additive manufacturing and pressureless sintering of ZrB2-MoSi2 ultra-high temperature ceramic (UHTC) composites for triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) heat exchangers intended for concentrating solar power applications. The binder used in the printing process (AquaFuse or PhenolFuse, ExOne) is an organic binder that is burned out at 600 degrees C at 2 degrees C/min with 2 h hold in flowing nitrogen, not a preceramic polymer. Sintering was performed at 2000 degrees C for 18 h in flowing argon achieving 92-98% theoretical density. Grain sizes were reported as generally less than 10 micrometers with larger print-defect pores on the order of tens of micrometers. Volumetric shrinkage upon sintering was approximately 60% and isotropic.

notes: Study investigates effects of cyclic (TMTVS) and cage (octavinyl-POSS) additives to base polysiloxane SPR-684 on SiOC ceramic properties. Additives ranged from 10-40 wt%. Pyrolysis performed at 1100°C, 1300°C, or 1400°C with water vapor injection (500-700°C) to encourage SiO2 formation. After pyrolysis, SiO2 nanodomains etched with 20 wt% HF for ~4 days to create micropores. PSO density after pyrolysis at 1100°C: 1.90 g/cm3. POSS addition increases specific surface area up to 1557 m2/g with pore size ~1.8 nm after etching. TMTVS addition decreases specific surface area and pore volume. Nitrogen adsorption at 77 K shows Type I isotherms (microporous). Molar vinyl:H ratios increase with additive loading: POSS samples 1.6-4.7; TMTVS samples 1.6-4.4. Additive ceramic yield for POSS: ~96.8-97.5%; for TMTVS: 58.1-91.4% decreasing with loading. Linear shrinkage: PSO ~21.1%; POSS additions reduce to 15.6% for 40P; TMTVS shows no strong trend (~19-22%). Pt catalyst loading: 1 wt% relative to PSO.
source: Effect of additive structure and size on SiO2 formation in polymer‐derived SiOC ceramics

notes: This paper is not primarily about a preceramic polymer; it concerns photopolymer binder systems used in lithography-based ceramic manufacturing (LCM/DLP) of 3Y-TZP zirconia ceramics. The binder polymers are (meth-)acrylates, not silicon-based preceramic polymers. System A (LithaCon 3Y230): mono/difunctional (meth-)acrylate binder, ~44 vol% ZrO2 solid loading, viscosity ~10.2 Pa·s at 30°C and 20 s⁻¹, exposure energy ~175 mJ/cm². System B (LithaCon 3Y210): multifunctional (meth-)acrylate binder, ~48 vol% ZrO2 solid loading, viscosity ~10.9 Pa·s at 30°C and 20 s⁻¹, exposure energy ~100 mJ/cm². Grain size midpoint of 440 nm reflects average of ~0.45 µm (A) and ~0.43 µm (B). Hardness midpoint 13.55 GPa reflects 13.5 (A) and 13.6 (B) GPa. Modulus midpoint 206 GPa reflects 207 (A) and 205 (B) GPa. Maximum wall thickness after sintering: ~6.2 mm (A) and ~4.7 mm (B).
source: Effect of binder system on the thermophysical properties of 3D‐printed zirconia ceramics

Beta-SiC lattice parameter: 4.365 A (SiC) vs 4.362 A (SiBC-5) at 1900C. Open porosity of SiBC-5 monolith at 1100C: 4.59%; at 1700C: 4.27%; at 1900C: 3.68%. Pure AHPCS shows single-step mass loss starting ~300 C, ending ~950 C, ceramic yield ~91.5%. 5 wt% BDMS sample yields ~94.8%, 20 wt% BDMS ~94.2%, 40 wt% BDMS ~92.7%. BDMS addition generally increases ceramic yield. Mass loss attributed to release of CnHm hydrocarbons and hydrogen. Pyrolysis temperatures studied: 1200, 1400, and 1600 C. No B4C crystalline phase detected even at 1600 C. B-C bonds confirmed by XPS at 190 eV (B1s) and 281.7 eV (C1s). SiC peaks shift to higher Bragg angle with boron doping indicating lattice contraction.

notes: Polymer precursor is SMP-10 (AHPCS, Starfire Systems) doped with 0-40 wt% borane dimethylsulfide (BDMS). Crosslinker: Karstedt's catalyst (0.05 wt%) for pure SiC; hydroboration reaction serves as crosslinking mechanism for boron-doped samples. Pyrolysis performed at 1200, 1400, and 1600 C for 2 h at 2 C/min in flowing Ar (99.99%). Beta-SiC crystallite sizes: pure AHPCS = 3 nm (1200 C), 3.2 nm (1400 C), 4.5 nm (1600 C); up to 11.7 nm at 40 wt% BDMS/1600 C. Graphitic carbon crystallite size (La) decreases with boron doping (e.g., 0 wt% BDMS at 1200 C: La=3.0 nm; 30 wt% BDMS at 1200 C: La=2.4 nm; 0 wt% BDMS at 1600 C: La=7.4 nm; 40 wt% BDMS at 1600 C: La=2.9 nm). Thermal stability at 2200 C also evaluated. Ceramic yield range for grain_size_nm and pyrolysis_temp_C reflect the highest pyrolysis temperature studied (1600 C) and the undoped AHPCS crystallite size at that temperature. Porosity reduction reported: ~22.42 vol% (pure SiC, PIP reference), reduced to 4.27 vol% with 5 wt% BDMS at 1700 C without PIP cycles (from cited prior work).
source: Effect of boron on phase, nanostructure, and thermal stability of polycarbosilane-derived SiC ceramics

notes: Study investigates effect of 3-pentanone solvent (0, 100, 200, 300 vol% relative to PSO) on SiOC phase evolution at pyrolysis temperatures 1100-1400 C. Solvent accelerates beta-SiC crystallization onset to 1100-1200 C range vs 1200-1300 C for pure PSO. Volume shrinkage ranges 24.25-53.52%. Bulk density ranges 1.05-1.84 g/cm3. Open porosity ranges 0.92-31.69%. 100-p samples showed anomalous behavior (expansion in thickness, cracking, low density, high porosity) attributed to inhomogeneous mixing and insufficient crosslinking. 200-p samples showed lowest porosity (0.92-6.47%) with high ceramic yield. Pentanone boiling point 102 C; crosslinking at 120 C performed in sealed acid digestion vessels. After crosslinking, samples aged at room temperature for 10 days. Pentanone remaining after aging: 21.98 wt% (100-p), 29.40 wt% (200-p), 30.99 wt% (300-p). XRD peak fitting used Pearson VII distributions. Manufacturer: Starfire Systems/Gelest Inc.

notes: This paper primarily studies ceramic SiOC/C products rather than the preceramic polymers themselves. Multiple precursors used: commercial resins (Polyramic SPR-212, SPR-684, SPR-688; BELSIL PMS-MK; SILRES 604) and sol-gel precursors (TREOS, MDES, TEMS, TEVS from Merck). Focus is on correlating free carbon content and ordering with charge carrier transport in SiOC ceramics. Percolation threshold varies from ~20 vol% C at 1100 C to ~6 vol% C at 1600 C. Three conduction regimes identified: insulating matrix dominance (<1 vol% C, Ea~1 eV), tunneling/hopping near percolation threshold, and weakly activated transport above percolation threshold (Ea=0.03 eV). Hall measurements indicate p-type carriers with mobility ~3 cm2/V and density 10^14 to 10^19 cm^-3. Crystallite size La = 7.5 nm at 1000-1500 C; crystallinity_state refers to the carbon phase at lower temperatures.
source: Effect of the Content and Ordering of the sp2 Free Carbon Phase on the Charge Carrier Transport in Polymer-Derived Silicon Oxycarbides

notes: Study focuses on addition of TEOS (0, 10, 20, 30, 40 wt%) to PSO polysiloxane precursor, pyrolysis in Ar+H2O atmosphere at 1100, 1300, or 1400°C, followed by HF etching to create porous SiOC. microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Pyrolysis yields amorphous SiOC matrix with mixed SiO4, SiOxC4-x, and SiC4 units. Transition metal addition (Fe, Co, Ni) induces formation of b-SiC, turbostratic/graphitic carbon, and metal silicides (Fe3Si, CoSi2). Phase separation of SiOC dominant over carbothermal reduction of SiO2+C. Catalytic graphitization activity order: Fe > Co > Ni. Activation energies for graphite growth: SiOC=66.64, SiOC/Ni=66.09, SiOC/Co=62.67, SiOC/Fe=60.72 kJ/mol.

notes: Study investigates catalytic graphitization of SiOC by Fe, Co, and Ni transition metals. Preceramic polymer is polysiloxane SPR-684 (Starfire Systems). Metal loading is 2 wt% each (Fe, Co, or Ni relative to polysiloxane). APTES used as complexing agent at metal:APTES = 1:4 molar ratio. Lateral graphite growth follows 2D grain growth (Hillert theory). XPS Si 2p analysis shows SiO4, SiO3C, SiO2C2, SiOC3, SiC4 units with atomic percentages reported at each temperature (Table 2). AD/AG Raman ratios decrease with temperature and with metal addition in order Fe > Co > Ni. Point-like defect density decreases with temperature and is lowest for SiOC/Fe. Phase separation of amorphous SiOC confirmed as dominant SiC formation mechanism over carbothermal reduction.
source: Effects of transition metals on the evolution of polymer-derived SiOC ceramics

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: SiOC ceramics contain amorphous SiO2 matrix, beta-SiC nanocrystallites, and free turbostratic/graphitic carbon. At 1000 °C: largely amorphous with SiO2 halo (~22°) and nascent SiC peak (35.7°). At 1200 °C: beta-SiC crystallization evident especially in PMPS-15PHMS; graphite peaks at 26.2° and 44.4°. At 1300-1400 °C: SiO2 remains amorphous (broad peak), beta-SiC peaks intensify at 35.7°, 41.5°, 60.1°, 71.9°. Phase separation expressed as SiOC -> amorphous SiO2 + beta-SiC + graphite above ~1300 °C.
