microstructural.ceramic_phase: SiOC with amorphous SiO2 nanodomains and turbostratic carbon
microstructural.phase_composition_notes: All pyrolyzed samples are amorphous by XRD. Two broad diffraction peaks at 43 degrees (turbostratic carbon) and 23 degrees (amorphous SiO2). SiO2 nanodomains form preferentially above 1100C. SiO2 domains selectively etched by HF to produce porous SiOC. Mixed Si-O-C tetrahedra (SiO1C3, SiO2C2, SiO3C1) present. SiC formation suppressed by water vapor atmosphere. After HF etching, etched density 0.52-0.55 g/cm3, average pore sizes 1.29-1.76 nm, specific pore volumes 0.75-1.34 cm3/g.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Volume shrinkage during pyrolysis 20.46-26.76% (range for all samples at 1100-1300C); shrinkage decreases with increasing PHPS filler content

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: amorphous SiO2 (broad peak ~23 degrees 2theta), turbostratic carbon (broad peak ~43 degrees 2theta); no SiC or crystalline carbon peaks detected even at 1300C

notes: Study investigates blending of PSO (SPR-684, Starfire Systems) with PHPS (NN 120-20, Clariant, 20 wt% in dibutyl ether) at Si molar ratios of 100:0, 100:1, 100:2, 100:5 (PSO:PHPS). Pt catalyst (2.1-2.4% platinum-divinyltetramethyldisiloxane in xylene, Gelest) used at 1 wt% relative to PSO. Pyrolysis at 1100, 1200, 1300C in Ar with H2O vapor injection (500-700C, Ar:H2O ~5:1). HF etching (20 wt% HF, 72h) removes SiO2 nanodomains to create porosity. Highest specific surface area achieved ~2000 m2/g at average pore size 1.72 nm for SiOC/PHPS-1 pyrolyzed at 1200C. Ceramic yields at 1200C: pure SiOC 64.9%, SiOC/PHPS-1 ~66.0% (at 1100C), SiOC/PHPS-5 ~60.4-55.5% (1100-1300C). Etching mass loss for pure SiOC at 1100C: 61.9 wt%. N2 adsorption (NLDFT) used for surface area and pore analysis. PHPS addition creates bimodal pore size distribution with small pores <2 nm (from SiOC phase-separated SiO2) and larger pores 2.3-5 nm (from PHPS evolution).
source: Porous and ultrahigh surface area SiOC ceramics based on perhydropolysilazane and polysiloxane

polymer_name: PMPHS (H62C, Wacker), PMPS (H44, Wacker), PMS (MK, Wacker), PHMS, Polyvinylsilazane (PVSZ) (Ceraset VL20, KiON), HTT 1800 (KiON), PCS (SMP-10, Starfire Systems), PDMS, PMHS (KF-99, Shin-etsu), PSX (YR3370, GE Toshiba Silicones), and others as listed in tables

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Pyrolysis temperatures reported across various studies range from 700 to 1600 C depending on polymer type and desired ceramic phase. Organic moiety elimination occurs via C-H bond breaking with release of H2, CH4, or other volatile compounds. General pyrolysis threshold stated as >800 C.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal (crosslinking temperatures mentioned at 190 C and 290 C for polysiloxane systems; UV and chemical crosslinking implied for other systems)

molecular_weight.measurement_method: Various Mw values cited for specific commercial products: PDMS 800-155000 g/mol (Gelest), PDMS 1700 g/mol (ABCR), PDMS-PEO 3100 g/mol (Dow Corning), PCS 800/1400/3500 g/mol (Sigma-Aldrich), PCS 1250 g/mol, PMHS 8000 g/mol (Shin-etsu), PHMS 1900 g/mol (Alfa Aesar)

backbone_architecture.description: Review paper covering multiple polymer types including polysiloxane, polycarbosilane, polysilazane, polyborazylene, and polyborosiloxane; no single backbone architecture described for a specific polymer

microstructural.ceramic_phase: SiOC, SiCN, SiC, SiBCN, SiBOC, Si3N4, BN, SiOCN, SiAlCN, SiTiOC, SiC-CDC, SiOC-CDC, SiCN-CDC
microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Nano-sized crystalline phases embedded in amorphous matrix containing free-carbon phase. Ceramic phase depends on polymer precursor type and pyrolysis temperature. SiC nanowires observed after pyrolysis at 1400 C via carbothermal reactions.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Compressive strengths reported for various porous ceramics: 0.42 MPa (SiBOC foam, 85 vol% porosity), 11-37 MPa (SiC/C from pinewood template), 1.1-1.6 MPa (SiC-TiC foams, 85-96 vol% porosity), 15-24 MPa (OM-SiOC, increasing with pyrolysis temperature), 1-9.4 MPa (self-foamed SiOC), 1-8 MPa (gas-blown SiOC), 50-58 MPa (emulsion-derived SiC)

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: SiC, Si3N4, BN identified in various systems after high-temperature pyrolysis; amorphous matrix typical for PDCs

notes: This is a review paper (Vakifahmetoglu, Zeydanli, Colombo, 2016) covering processing strategies for porous ceramics derived from preceramic polymers. It does not report data for a single specific polymer but surveys many polymer precursors and processing methods including: replica technique (soft and hard templating), sacrificial agents, preceramic polymer mixtures, preceramic polymer decomposition, blowing (self-foaming, physical/chemical blowing agents, gas blowing), etching (HF solution, halogen gases), freeze casting, emulsions, aerogels, automated manufacturing, and spinning techniques. Ceramic products include SiOC, SiCN, SiC, SiBCN, SiBOC, Si3N4, BN, SiOCN, and others. Porosity ranges from ~1 to 96 vol%; pore sizes from sub-nanometer to millimeter scale; SSA from <1 to >3000 m2/g depending on processing route. Multiple commercial polymer products referenced including Wacker MK, H44, HTT 1800 (KiON), Ceraset VL20 (KiON), SMP-10 (Starfire Systems).
source: Porous polymer derived ceramics

bonding_structure.other_bonds: C-S bonds (thioether, ~1.83 Å), C-N bonds (pyridine, 1300-1600 cm-1), Si-O-Si backbone (~1020 cm-1), Si-CH at 950 cm-1

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: PyMPS is used as a preceramic polymer in nanocomposite development; the ceramic phase after pyrolysis is not characterized in this study. Nanoparticle filler is Cu2S (P21/c monoclinic, ICSD CIF #100333)

notes: This paper focuses on PyMPS as a preceramic polymer used in a one-pot 'pre-ceramic polymer-assisted nucleation and growth' (PPANG) synthesis of Cu2S nanoparticles. PyMPS serves simultaneously as reducing agent, sulfur donor, capping ligand, and shape-directing agent. Cu2S nanoplate size range is 3.4-9.7 nm by Rietveld refinement (midpoint ~6.55 nm noted in grain_size_nm); SAXS Rg ranges from 55-61 Å depending on PyMPS:oleylamine ratio. No pyrolysis or PDC ceramic conversion data is reported in this paper. FTIR characteristic peaks: 1300-1600 cm-1 (C-N), 1250 cm-1 (Si-CH3), 1020 cm-1 (Si-O-Si), 950 cm-1 (Si-CH), 820 cm-1 (Si-C). PDF peaks: ~1.5 Å (Si-O and Si-C/C-C), ~1.8 Å (Si-C and C-S). PyMPS synthesis referenced from prior work (ref. 22). Reaction atmosphere: argon. Nanoparticle synthesis temperature: 200°C, held 1 h; heating rate ~6°C/min to final temperature.
source: Pre-ceramic polymer-assisted nucleation and growth of copper sulfide nanoplates

notes: This is an editorial overview for a special issue of the Journal of the American Ceramic Society on preceramic polymers. It contains no experimental data, specific polymer characterization, or measured properties. It broadly references silicon-based PDC materials and applications including high-temperature fibers, coatings, porous structures, dense monoliths, additive manufacturing, energy systems, aerospace, microelectronics, and biomedicine, but provides no quantitative descriptors for any specific polymer.
source: Preceramic polymers-Unlocking new horizons in advanced ceramics

elemental_composition.other_elements: AMF2p: Si4.46BC7.32N4.40; AMF3p: Si2.72BC4.51N2.69; T2/1p: Si3.08BC4.39N2.28 (atomic ratios, not percentages)

bonding_structure.other_bonds: Boron trigonally coordinated by nitrogen (BN3) as indicated by NMR studies; B-N bonds present

functional_groups.other: T2/1 synthesized by hydroboration of dichloromethylvinylsilane and subsequent ammonolysis; AMF2/AMF3 synthesized by ammonolysis of dichloromethylvinylsilane to yield oligomethylvinylsilazane, then reacted with borane dimethylsulfide

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Thermolysis leads to decrease in hydrogen and carbon content; Si/B/N atomic ratios remain constant after thermolysis; ceramics are amorphous after thermolysis at 1400°C; extraordinary high-temperature stability up to 2000°C reported

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: All samples X-ray amorphous after thermolysis at 1400°C. Nominal phase contents: AMF2p = Si3N4 + 2.3SiC + 1.2BN + 6.3C; AMF3p = Si3N4 + 6.6SiC + 3.1BN + 7.0C; T2/1p = Si3N4 + 3.4SiC + 2.4BN + 7.2C. Raman spectra show G and D bands indicating graphite-like carbon on nanometer scale. No significant crystallization observed after oxidation at 1500°C for 75 h.

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: All samples X-ray amorphous after thermolysis; no crystallization detected after oxidation at 1500°C for 75 h by Raman spectroscopy

notes: This paper focuses primarily on oxidation behavior of precursor-derived SiBCN ceramics rather than polymer characterization. Three ceramics studied: AMF2p, AMF3p, T2/1p. Oxidation at 1300° and 1500°C for up to 100 h in air and oxygen. Parabolic rate constants at 1500°C in air: AMF3p = 0.0599 µm²/h, T2/1p = 0.0593 µm²/h; AMF2p does not follow parabolic law. Scale thicknesses smaller than CVD-SiC or CVD-Si3N4. Oxide scales remain amorphous (no cristobalite crystallization) attributed to boron incorporation. Specific surface area below 0.1 m²/g. AMF2 has reduced boron content relative to AMF3 and T2/1.
source: Precursor-Derived Si-B-C-N Ceramics- Oxidation Kinetics

bonding_structure.other_bonds: B-H present (IR: 2509 cm-1), B-N present (IR: 1435 cm-1), B-N-B bending (890 cm-1), BH bending (690 cm-1); 11B MAS NMR shows BN2H at 31 ppm and BN3 at 27 ppm

functional_groups.other: B-H hydride groups on boron; N-H groups on nitrogen; borazine-derived ring structures (six-membered and eight-membered rings, naphthalene-like borazine derivatives)

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: TGA in N2 to 1000 °C at 5 °C/min: 25-70 °C Δm=0%; 70-280 °C Δm=4.5%; 290-750 °C Δm=3.5%; 750-1000 °C Δm=1.1%. Total weight loss ~9.1%. Additional pyrolysis steps performed at 1600 and 1800 °C (2 h hold, 0.5 °C/min ramp) in nitrogen.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal - self-condensation of borazine at 60 °C in autoclave under static argon for ~240 h; degree of cross-linking controlled by polymerization temperature and dwelling time

backbone_architecture.description: Branched-chain or partially cross-linked structure formed by ring condensation of borazine forming naphthalene-like (biphenyl/naphthalenic-type) borazine derivatives with H2 release. Contains six-membered borazine rings and eight-membered rings.

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: After pyrolysis at 1450 °C: B3.0N2.95O0.04, relative density 86.3%. After pyrolysis at 1800 °C: B3.0N2.9, relative density ~93%. XRD confirmed h-BN phase (JCPDS 34-0421). Crystallite sizes increase with temperature: Lhc from 2.35 nm (as-prepared) to 8.60 nm (1800 °C); Lha from 7.26 nm to 35.6 nm.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Warm-pressed at 74 MPa at 60 °C into disk-shaped green bodies (13 mm diameter, 2.6 mm thickness). Glass transition temperature range 88-120 °C. TMA performed under 0.8 N compressive load.

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN), JCPDS 34-0421; (002) and (100) reflections identified

notes: Polymer synthesized by self-condensation of borazine (B3N3H6) at 60 °C in a 75 mL autoclave under static argon for ~240 h, reaching internal pressure of 121.1 bar. Yielded ~15.2 g of white solid powder from 17.8 g borazine. Polymer milled and sieved to ≤80 μm before warm-pressing. DSC performed in argon between -50 and 150 °C at 10 °C/min. 11B MAS NMR recorded at 9.4 T, 128.28 MHz, 12.5 kHz spinning, spin-echo sequence, referenced to BF3(OEt)2. Two other polyborazylenes (1 and 2) were prepared at 45 °C and 50 °C respectively but were liquid and not suitable for warm-pressing. XRD d002 values: 0.352 nm (as-prepared), 0.339 nm (1600 °C), 0.338 nm (1800 °C). Crystallite sizes at 1450 °C: Lhc=7.15 nm, Lha=25.57 nm; at 1800 °C: Lhc=8.60 nm, Lha=35.6 nm.
source: Preparation of Polyborazylene-Derived Bulk Boron Nitride with Tunable Properties by Warm-Pressing and Pressureless Pyrolysis

polymer_name: SMP-10 (allyl hydrido polycarbosilane, Star Fire Systems)

elemental_composition.other_elements: Oxygen reported as 3-6.7 wt% in polymer; carbon 34-35 wt% and oxygen 3-4 wt% in ceramic from liquid SMP-10 pyrolysis. Allyl groups present at 4.8 mol%.

bonding_structure.other_bonds: Allyl groups (Si-CH2-CH=CH2) present at 4.8 mol%; Si-H band at ~2121 cm-1; allyl bands at 1631 and 3070 cm-1. Crosslinking via hydrosilylation and dehydrocoupling reactions.

functional_groups.other: Allyl groups (4.8 mol%); large excess of Si-H groups relative to allyl groups

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Decomposition occurs in two major steps. First step T<250C: hydrogen and small polymer fragments evolve via hydrosilylation (zero mass change). Second major step 400-850C: release of H2 (m/z=2), SiH4 (m/z=32), CH3SiH3 (m/z=46). Polymer-to-ceramic transformation complete by 800-850C. Ceramic yield ~77 wt%.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal - hydrosilylation (at T<=250C) and dehydrocoupling reactions (at T>250C, major at 300-650C)

backbone_architecture.description: Allyl hydrido polycarbosilane; liquid at room temperature (clear, amber-colored, viscous liquid); requires no solvents for processing. Crosslinks thermally to infusible solid via hydrosilylation and dehydrocoupling.

microstructural.ceramic_phase: SiC (beta-SiC primary phase, with minor alpha-SiC at high temperatures; X-ray amorphous at 1300C and below)
microstructural.phase_composition_notes: At 1050-1300C: X-ray amorphous, excess carbon and oxygen present, amorphous silica formed. At 1500-1700C: beta-SiC crystallizes with minor alpha-SiC. Near-stoichiometric SiC at 1700C due to carbothermal reduction of silica. Empirical formulas at different temperatures given in tables (e.g., SiC1.02O0.01 at 1700C for sample 17SiC). Samples not fully crystalline even at high temperature.

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: beta-SiC (primary), alpha-SiC (minor) at 1500-1700C; X-ray amorphous at 1300C

notes: Paper focuses on fabrication of dense SiC monoliths via polymer processing of SMP-10. Process: (1) thermal curing of liquid SMP-10 at <=250C to powder, (2) ball milling, (3) uniaxial warm-pressing at 300C/127.4 MPa to green body, (4) pyrolysis at 1050C in argon, (5) annealing at up to 1700C in argon. PIP technique applied for porosity reduction: after 6 cycles porosity ~0.49 vol% at 1050C. Skeletal density of ceramics: 2.63-2.69 g/cm3. Mass loss and porosity increase with annealing temperature due to CO release (carbothermal reduction). Oxygen in ceramic (5-6 wt%) attributed partly to warm-pressing step exposing material to air. Porosity range in tables: 12.37-22.42 vol% depending on annealing temperature; maximum porosity 22.42 vol% reported for 17SiC at 1700C. Pyrolysis at 1050C with 2h hold (11SiC sample); subsequent annealing at 1300, 1500, 1700C for 3h hold. Green body optimized process: pre-compaction at RT ~127 MPa, pressure release, then pressureless crosslinking at 300C.
source: Pressureless fabrication of dense monolithic SiC ceramics from a polycarbosilane

elemental_composition.other_elements: Elemental composition given in wt% for polymer RD-684: Si 22.65%, O 13.10%, C 57.45%, H 6.00% (empirical formula SiOC5.84H7.32). Atomic percentages not directly reported.

bonding_structure.other_bonds: Vinyl groups present on polysiloxane backbone; hydrosilylation and dehydrocoupling reactions noted during crosslinking

functional_groups.other: Phenyl groups inferred from mass spectrometry detection of phenyl fragments (m/z=50,51,52,77,78) during pyrolysis; propyl fragments also detected

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: TGA performed at 5 deg C/min in argon up to 1400 deg C; total weight loss 40 wt% occurring in two main decomposition steps between 350 and 750 deg C; evolved gases include hydrocarbons (vinyl, phenyl, methyl, propyl fragments) and hydrogen detected by in situ QMS. Actual ceramic part weight loss was ~35 wt%, lower than TGA value (40 wt%), attributed to increased crosslinking from additional UV irradiation. Ceramic yield ~60 wt% for parts (complement of 40 wt% TGA loss noted; part loss 35 wt%).

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: UV/photoinitiated radical crosslinking at 365 nm using Irgacure 651 (5 wt%) photoinitiator; vinyl polymerization, hydrosilylation, and dehydrocoupling mechanisms involved; 20 min initial irradiation plus 10 min per side additional irradiation

backbone_architecture.description: Commercially available polysiloxane that forms a three-dimensional infusible network upon UV-initiated crosslinking via vinyl polymerization, hydrosilylation, and dehydrocoupling reactions

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Samples pyrolyzed at 1100 deg C are X-ray amorphous. Sample at 1400 deg C contains turbostratic graphite-like phase and silicon carbide as crystalline phases confirmed by XRD, TEM, and Raman. Very high free carbon content: 78-86 mol% segregated free carbon. At 1100 deg C estimated composition: ~31 wt% amorphous SiO2, ~11 wt% amorphous SiC, ~58 wt% segregated carbon.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Vickers hardness range 5.5-8.6 GPa (midpoint 7.05 GPa) measured under loads 0.5-20 N. Young's modulus measured by nanoindentation (Berkovich indenter, max load 300 mN) but value not reported numerically in extracted text. DC resistivity at 1100 deg C: 0.35 ohm·m; at 1400 deg C: 0.14 ohm·m.

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: Samples at 1100 deg C: X-ray amorphous. Sample at 1400 deg C: turbostratic graphite-like phase and SiC crystalline phases identified by XRD, TEM, and Raman spectroscopy.

notes: Hardness range 5.5-8.6 GPa; midpoint 7.05 GPa used, range noted. Pyrolysis also performed at 1000 deg C and 1400 deg C for elemental analysis comparison. Ceramic density 1.6-1.7 g/cm3, unusually low due to high carbon content. BET surface area <1 m2/g indicating fully dense non-porous material. Linear shrinkage upon pyrolysis ~20%. Maximum crack-free monolith dimensions: 3.4 cm diameter, 1.5 mm thickness. Irgacure 651 photoinitiator addition increased carbon content in ceramic from 51.56 wt% (without) to 61.19 wt% (with). Paper: Journal of the European Ceramic Society 31 (2011) 913-919, Martínez-Crespiera et al.
source: Pressureless synthesis of fully dense and crack-free SiOC bulk ceramics via photo-crosslinking and pyrolysis of a polysiloxane

bonding_structure.other_bonds: Si-N stretching at 970 cm-1, Si-C stretching at 812 cm-1, C=N stretching at 1720 cm-1, C-N stretching at 1253 and 1188 cm-1, C(sp3)-H bands at 2924 and 2860 cm-1, free carbon bands at 1652, 1583, 1503, 1447, 1378 cm-1. Backbone contains Si-N=C=N (silylcarbodiimide) linkages.

functional_groups.other: phenyl groups on Si; carbodiimide (-N=C=N-) groups in backbone; borane (from hydroboration of vinyl groups) in HN1B

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Two pyrolysis temperatures used: 1100 C (heating rate 100 C/h = 1.67 C/min, 2h hold) and 1400 C (heating rate 5 C/min, 2h hold, cooling at 10 C/min). Carbothermal reaction observed at 1400 C: a-Si3N4 + 3 a-C -> 3 alpha/beta-SiC + 2N2. Powder ceramics show more N loss and SiC crystallization at 1400 C compared to bulk ceramics.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal (precrosslinking of HN1 at 255 C for 5h; warm pressing at 200 C/26 MPa/2h for HN1 and 220 C/88 MPa/2h for HN1B)

backbone_architecture.description: Polysilylcarbodiimide backbone -[R1R2Si-N=C=N]n- with R1=phenyl, R2=vinyl for HN1. HN1B obtained by hydroboration of HN1 vinyl groups with borane dimethylsulphide, introducing boron into the network. Precrosslinked HN1 forms a powder retaining residual vinyl groups.

microstructural.ceramic_phase: SiCN / SiBCN; amorphous at 1100 C; partial crystallization at 1400 C
microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Pyrolysis of carbon-rich polysilylcarbodiimides yields three amorphous phases: a-Si3N4, a-SiC, and a-C (free carbon). At 1400 C, powder ceramics show crystallization of SiC and loss of Si3N4 via carbothermal reaction. Bulk ceramics show improved thermal stability against crystallization compared to powders. A SiCN(O) surface layer ~3 um thick forms on bulk ceramics. Free carbon present as graphene-like (turbostratic) carbon clusters.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Bulk ceramics described as compact and mechanically stable green bodies. Warm pressing conditions: HN1 at 200 C, 26 MPa, 2h; HN1B at 220 C, 88 MPa, 2h.

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: X-ray amorphous at 1100 C; at 1400 C powder samples show alpha/beta-SiC crystallization; bulk samples remain more amorphous at 1400 C

notes: Study compares powder vs. bulk processing routes for carbon-rich SiCN (HN1) and SiBCN (HN1B) PDCs. Raman D/G band ratios and carbon cluster sizes (La) reported: La ranges from ~1.4 to 2.4 nm across samples. LD (inter-defect distance) ranges from ~5.7 to 9.9 nm. Bulk ceramics show improved crystallization resistance vs. powders. HN1B (boron-containing) shows further enhanced thermal stability. Pyrolysis at 1100 C used heating rate of 100 C/h (1.67 C/min); post-annealing to 1400 C used 5 C/min ramp. SiBCN ceramics stable up to 2000-2200 C in inert atmosphere per cited literature. Empirical formulas for ceramics given in table.
source: Processing route dramatically influencing the nanostructure of carbon-rich SiCN and SiBCN polymer-derived ceramics. Part I- Low temperature thermal transformation

bonding_structure.other_bonds: Si-CH2-Si backbone linkage observed at 1356 and 1028 cm-1; epoxy oxirane C-O-C stretching at 831 cm-1 present in EMPCS; C-H stretching of epoxy methylene group at 3057 cm-1 in EMPCS

functional_groups.other: Epoxy (oxirane) groups present in EMPCS variants; epoxy resin LY556 grade used as modifier

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: PCS ceramic yield ~67%; 10EMPCS yield ~75%; 20EMPCS yield ~73%. Below 400 °C EMPCS shows higher weight loss than PCS; above 400 °C PCS decomposes faster. Weight loss begins around 250 °C attributed to escape of lower molecular weight fractions. TGA flow rate 0.5 ml/min argon. Foaming and ceramization performed separately: foaming at 1000 °C under N2 at 2 °C/min, then ceramization at 1200/1400/1600 °C under vacuum at 1-2 °C/min with 2 h hold.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal - PCS crosslinks above 300 °C during heating; epoxy modification alters crosslinking behavior

backbone_architecture.description: Polycarbosilane synthesized by thermal backbone rearrangement of polydimethylsilane (PDMS); Si-CH2-Si backbone with Si-CH3 and Si-H pendant groups; modified with epoxy resin LY556 by refluxing in THF at 150 °C. Mn reported as 1300-1500 g/mol range.

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: SiC foam produced after ceramization at 1200, 1400, and 1600 °C under vacuum; phase composition analyzed by XRD. Higher ceramization temperature increases compressive strength.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Compressive strength values: 10EMPCS foam - 2.2 MPa (1200°C), 2.5 MPa (1400°C), 3.8 MPa (1600°C); 20EMPCS foam - 1.9 MPa (1200°C), 2.1 MPa (1400°C), 2.9 MPa (1600°C). Strength increases with ceramization temperature and decreases with increasing porosity. PCS-only foam too brittle to test.

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: SiC (confirmed by XRD; specific phases/peaks not detailed in provided text)

notes: Mn range given as 1300-1500 g/mol; midpoint 1400 used. Ceramic yield range: PCS ~67%, 10EMPCS ~75%, 20EMPCS ~73%; midpoint of all three used as representative value (71.7%). Porosity range for foams: PCS-based 81.8%, 10EMPCS-based 87%, 20EMPCS-based 90.6% at 1600°C. Bulk densities: PCS 0.6 g/cc, 10EMPCS 0.4 g/cc, 20EMPCS 0.3 g/cc at 1600°C. Cell sizes 100-700 µm in ceramized foams. EMPCS synthesized by refluxing PCS and epoxy LY556 in THF at 150°C. Foaming conducted at 1000°C under N2; ceramization at 1200/1400/1600°C under vacuum (100 mbar) with 2h hold. Thermal insulation test: 20EMPCS SiC foam (10mm thick) exposed to oxy-acetylene flame 120s; back face temperature ~300°C.
source: Processing, properties and microstructure of SiC foam derived from epoxymodified polycarbosilane

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Primary focus is on SiC ceramic and Si-SiC composites; some RB-SiC (reaction bonded SiC) with residual Si noted

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Various bending strengths reported for AM-fabricated SiC components ranging from ~9.74 MPa to 390 MPa depending on AM method and post-processing; modulus values of 356-458 GPa reported for selected composites

notes: This paper is a review article on additive manufacturing of SiC ceramics, not a preceramic polymer chemistry paper. It does not describe a specific preceramic polymer. Polymer precursors (e.g., phenolic resin, PF resin) are mentioned only as binders or coatings to facilitate SLS or as part of PIP post-processing steps. No preceramic polymer characterization data (composition, molecular weight, TGA, bonding structure, etc.) is reported. All preceramic polymer descriptor fields are null because the paper does not characterize any specific preceramic polymer.
source: Progress and challenges towards additive manufacturing of SiC ceramic

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: ZrB2-SiC and ZrB2-MoSi2 composites; SiC content varied 0-30 vol%; MoSi2 content varied 0-30 vol%; reactive hot pressing produced ZrB2-SiC from ZrH2, Si, and B4C precursors

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Fracture toughness reported: ZrB2-30vol%SiC = 5.3 MPa*m^0.5; ZrB2-30vol%MoSi2 = 4.0 MPa*m^0.5; reactive hot pressed ZrB2-SiC strength ~800 MPa at 1650C; non-catastrophic failure demonstrated in fibrous monolithic ceramics

notes: This paper is not about preceramic polymers. It concerns ultra-high temperature ceramics (UHTCs), specifically ZrB2-based ceramics and composites, processed by conventional hot pressing, co-extrusion, pressureless sintering, and reactive hot pressing. No preceramic polymer descriptors are applicable. Reactive hot pressing used ZrH2, Si, and B4C powders to form ZrB2-SiC. Grain sizes reported in micrometers: RHP ZrB2-SiC ~1.5 um at 1750C; conventionally HP ZrB2-SiC ~3 um at 1900C. Relative densities >99% achieved for ZrB2-30vol%SiC by conventional hot pressing.
source: Reactive Processing and Co-Extrusion-of Ultra-High Temperature Ceramics and Composites

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Pyrolysis weight loss approximately 74-75 wt% for beech and pine wood, and 74 wt% for rattan; linear shrinkage was anisotropic. Biocarbon preforms subsequently infiltrated with Si-Mo eutectic melt at 1500°C for 30 min under vacuum (<10^-2 Pa) with heating/cooling rate of 10°C/min.

Self-assembly morphology is solvent-dependent: THF gives hexagonally packed cylinders (PNB cylinders in PDB matrix); chloroform gives lamellae. notes: Three siloxane oligomer precursors (DDTS, DTDS, TPTS) were electrospun with 10 wt% PVP (Mw ~1,300,000 g/mol) as spinning agent in isopropanol (weight ratio siloxane:PVP = 3:1) and crosslinked with 1 wt% DCP. Electrochemical performance as LIB anode: best capacity 866 mA h/g (total electrode) at 50 mA/g, 72% first-cycle coulombic efficiency; 800 mA h/g at 50 mA/g with 100% retention after 50 cycles for one sample. As supercapacitor: 55 F/g at 100 mV/s, 100% capacitance retention over 5000 cycles at 3 A/g. Elemental compositions reported are for pyrolyzed ceramic products by XPS, not the precursor polymers. notes: This is a broad review paper on polymer-derived ceramics (PDCs) for energy conversion and storage applications, not a focused study on a single preceramic polymer. Specific quantitative polymer characterization data (elemental composition, molecular weight, ceramic yield, etc.) for individual polymers are not reported in the extracted text. The paper covers polysilazanes, polycarbosilanes, polysiloxanes, poly(silylcarbodiimides), and polyborosilazanes as precursor classes. Crosslinking temperature range: 100-400 C for shaping; ceramization: 400-1400 C. Crystallization and phase separation occur at or above 1400 C. SiCN from polysilylcarbodiimides crystallizes 50-100 C higher than SiCN from polysilazanes at analogous C/Si ratios. Named commercial polymers referenced include KiON HTT1800, Durazane 1800, ABSE polysilazane, and perhydropolysilazane used as coating precursors. Coating pyrolysis temperatures range from 700 to 1400 C depending on substrate and precursor system.

The study focuses on joining of pre-formed alpha-beta Yb-SiAlON ceramic pieces (TK4, Kennametal). Application of mechanical load during pyrolysis (via graphite fixture thermal expansion mismatch) was essential for robust joints. Pre-oxidation of SiAlON at 1300 degrees C in air for 3 h improved wetting but showed no significant benefit on final microstructure. Selected samples treated at 1570 degrees C showed improved integration of joint into parent ceramic. Polymer Tg slightly below 100 degrees C. notes: Paper focuses primarily on electronic properties of polymer-derived SiCN and SiBCN ceramics rather than polymer characterization. Two precursor systems described: (1) polyhydridomethylsilazane NCP 200 for SiCN ceramics, (2) 2:1 tris[dichloromethylsilyl]ethyl]borane polymer for SiBCN ceramics. Boron doping leads to p-type conductivity ~0.1 V^-1 cm^-1 at room temperature for SiBCN vs ~10^-10 (V cm)^-1 for pristine SiCN. Both SiCN and SiBCN exhibit Mott 3D variable range hopping conductivity. SiBCN thermopower is low and positive (~1 μV/K), attributed to compensation of n-type N doping by B-induced holes. Structural analysis by RRDF shows local Si tetrahedral structure with B, C, N at corners. Boron retards atomic mobility and preserves amorphous state to >1800 °C.

notes: The preceramic polymer SR350 is a thermosetting methyl-hydroxyl-siloxane (polysiloxane) used to produce SiOC ceramic open-cell foams via co-blowing with polyurethane precursors and pyrolysis at 1000-1400°C in N2 (heating rate 2 K/min, 1 h hold). Ceramic yield of SR350 is ~85%. Weight ratio preceramic polymer/polyurethane in foam was 1/1. Sub-micron beta-SiC powder (H.C. Starck B10, 0.3-0.5 µm) added at SiC/SR350 weight ratio of 1/4, corresponding to ~30 wt% SiC in final ceramic foam. Dichloromethane used as mutual solvent and physical blowing agent. Pre-heating at 400°C in air before pyrolysis reduced free carbon content to 12.44 wt%. CTE (25-1000°C): 0.5×10-6 K-1 (flexible PU foams), 1.5×10-6 K-1 (semi-rigid PU foams), 1.36×10-6 K-1 (SiOC+SiC foams). notes: Paper focuses on electrical characterisation of polysilazane-derived SiCN ceramics rather than polymer chemistry details. Grain size range given as 2-5 nm (midpoint 3.5 nm used). DC conductivity controllable over 15 orders of magnitude (10^-15 to 1 (ohm cm)^-1) by temperature, atmosphere, and annealing time. Charge transport in amorphous SiCN attributed to large polaron tunnelling; in crystalline SiC/Si3N4 attributed to electron transport in conduction band of N-doped SiC. Donor level Ed = 0.067 eV derived from conductivity measurements. Thermopower ~10 microV/K at room temperature (n-type). Cole-Cole parameters and fitting parameters reported in tables for annealing temperatures 1100-1300C. Isothermal annealing times of 25-50 h mentioned. Paper is Part II of a series; Part I (Refs. 7-9) describes synthesis and phase transformations in detail.

notes: This paper does not describe a preceramic polymer system. It concerns the fabrication of open-cell Si3N4 ceramic foams via emulsification of aqueous Si3N4 powder slurries with octane as the alkane phase, followed by rapid pressureless sintering using a modified SPS setup (PLSPS). No preceramic polymer is used as a precursor. The porosity ranged from 79 to 86 vol% depending on octane concentration (50 or 70 vol%) and stirring rate (700 or 1000 rpm). Sintering was conducted at 1600 C under vacuum. SiC nanowires (~150 nm diameter) decorated cell walls, formed via a catalyst-assisted VLS mechanism. Average grain size for alpha-Si3N4 was 1.7 um (PLSPS) vs 3.7 um (conventional sintering). Modulus and flexural strength values of 310 GPa and 900 MPa are for dense Si3N4 cited from literature, not measured in this study. Porosity midpoint of 82.5 vol% noted in microstructural field; range was 79-86 vol%.

Sol-gel systems can be tuned from highly cross-linked networks (basic conditions) to elongated chains (acidic conditions).

notes: This is a review paper on silicon oxycarbide (SiOC) glasses and glass-ceramics derived from polysiloxanes and sol-gel alkoxysilane precursors, not a study of a single specific polymer. Polysilsesquioxanes have general formula [RSiO1.5]n. Boron incorporation via boric acid or borane dimethyl sulfide complex modification of polysiloxanes is described. notes: This is a comprehensive review paper covering many different polysilazane types and their derived ceramics. Values reported span multiple polymers and processing conditions. Key commercially available polysilazanes discussed include: Ceraset SZ (PUMVS), Tonen NN110/310/710 (PHPS and variants), Gelest PSN series, Hochst ET70/VT50, Nichimen NCP100/200, and Bayer oligoborosilazane/polyborosilazane. Pyrolysis ceramic yield midpoint of 67.5% and pyrolysis temp of 1100 C are rough midpoints across the range of systems discussed; actual values vary significantly by polymer. Boron-modified polyborosilazanes yield Si/B/C/N ceramics with stability to 2000 C. The review also covers CVD, fibre spinning, coatings, and powder processing applications.

notes: The polymer HTT 1800 is a commercial polysilazane containing Si-H and Si-vinyl groups. It was modified in two steps: first with Hf(NEt2)4 (10 or 30 vol% relative to HTT 1800), then with BH3·SMe2, to form a single-source precursor for SiHfBCN ceramics. Crosslinking at 200°C produced yellow solids, which were warm-pressed at 260°C and 63 MPa, then pyrolyzed at 1100°C (heating rate 50°C/h, dwell 2h) in Ar to yield amorphous SiHfBCN ceramic monoliths. Annealing was performed at 1300, 1500, and 1700°C in Ar or N2. Elemental analysis of selected samples (SiHfBCN2a/2b) showed wt% values: C ~11-21%, O ~0.9-2.4%, N ~0.4-23.8%, Hf ~22.5-28.6% (by EDS). Raman spectroscopy data on free carbon phase provided; Leq and LD values in nm range indicating nanoscale graphene-like carbon domains. Phase separation (SiC4 + SiN4 from SiCxN4-x) was detected by 29Si NMR at temperatures as low as 800°C, which is unusual for SiCN/SiBCN ceramics. The ceramic yield of ~80 wt% is notably higher than HTT 1800 alone (~65 wt%) due to increased crosslinking from Hf and B modification. Heating rate for crosslinking: 50°C/h = ~0.83°C/min.

Polysilazane is mentioned as one of several preceramic polymers (including silazane, alkylsilazanes, hexamethyldisilazane, methylhexamethyldisilazane, hexamethylcyclotrisilazane, octamethylcyclotetrasilazane, polyureamethylvinylsilazanes, polyvinysilazane) used in polymer-derived ceramic routes for Si3N4. Wang et al. [60] specifically used polysilazane mixed with epoxy resin for DLP printing, pyrolyzed at 1600 C to achieve 70% crystallinity. Siloxane was also mentioned as a precursor pyrolyzed in nitrogen-rich environment to form Si3N4-based felts. Most quantitative polymer characterization data are absent as this is a review paper.

elemental_composition.other_elements: Elemental compositions reported as wt% and mole ratios for multiple polymer/ceramic samples in tables. thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: TGA performed under flowing nitrogen with ~30mg samples. Mass loss products identified at different temperature ranges: 70-250°C silazane oligomers released; 250-450°C larger silazane fragments plus CH3NH2 and SiH4; 450-600°C CH4 (major), C2H4, C2H6, C3H6, C3H8, CH3CN, CH3CH=NH. Bulk pyrolysis to 800°C with 3h hold. Some samples subsequently heated to 1600°C at ~10°C/min under static nitrogen at ~100 kPa (increasing to ~700 kPa at 1600°C). Ceramic yields vary widely by polymer type: phenyl-substituted 50-69 wt%, hexyl-substituted 24-36 wt%, ONMS 41-50 wt%, PNMS 49-61 wt%.

molecular_weight.measurement_method: Vapour-phase osmometry (VPO), size exclusion chromatography (SEC). ONMS starting material: Mn=1100, Mw=4000, Mz=13000 daltons; after further catalytic reaction: Mn=2300, Mw=23600, Mz=128000 daltons. Phenyl polymer Mn values from table: 800, 1220, 1600 daltons; hexyl polymer Mn: 850, 2210 daltons (before pyrolysis).

backbone_architecture.description: Products include linear and cyclo-oligomers. Polymers described as slightly branched or containing cages or rings as desirable. Backbone unit -[H2SiNCH3]- described as monomeric prototype. Catalytic dehydrocoupling of Si-H with N-H bonds used for synthesis. Ring-opening polymerization also noted.

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Pyrolysis at 800°C yields amorphous silicon-based ceramics. Heating to 1600°C causes crystallization. Target ceramic is Si3N4; SiC also formed when Si-CH3 groups present. XRD used for phase identification of 1600°C products. Ceramic elemental compositions approach Si3N4 stoichiometry at 1600°C (e.g. ONMS run 3: C 13.1, H 0.1, N 34.1, Si 53.2, O 0.5 wt%; hexyl run 10 mole ratio N/Si=1.25).

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Viscosity of ONMS starting material: 5P; after further catalytic reaction: 98P. Rheometry mentioned as analytical method. Tenacity of preceramic fibres discussed qualitatively.

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: Powder X-ray diffraction used for phase identification of products pyrolyzed at 800°C (amorphous) and 1600°C (crystallized). Specific crystalline phases not enumerated in extracted text but implied to be Si3N4 and/or SiC.

notes: Paper studies multiple polysilazane types: (1) phenylsilane+NH3 derived (PPS, short and long reaction times), (2) hexylsilane+NH3 derived (PHS), (3) oligo(N-methylsilazane) ONMS, and (4) poly(N-methylsilazane) PNMS. All synthesized by ruthenium-catalyzed dehydrocoupling (Ru3(CO)12 catalyst). Oxygen contamination generally below 1 wt% in most materials. Ceramic yields increase with longer reaction time/higher Mn. Hexyl-substituted polymers give significantly lower ceramic yields than phenyl or N-methyl substituted polymers. Si-CH3 groups noted to consistently produce SiC along with Si3N4 upon pyrolysis under inert atmosphere. Standard bulk pyrolysis: 0.5°C/min to 800°C, hold 3h, flowing nitrogen at 60 ml/min. High-temperature treatment: ~10°C/min to 1600°C, static nitrogen ~100 kPa. Multiple MS techniques used: GC-MS, Knudsen cell MS, Py/FIMS, TPR-MS.

notes: Study investigates two PCS types (PCS and StarPCS SMP-10, Starfire Systems, Schenectady, NY) dissolved in toluene for dip-coating 3D-printed wood-filament preforms to fabricate SiC ceramics. Nano-sized SiC was also added to solutions. Pre-ceramic pastes (5A, 5A Nano1, 5A Nano2) contain phenolic resins, carbon powders, SiC powders (nano- to micro-scale), micro-scale Si powders, active refractory ceramic fillers, coupling agents, dispersants, and surfactants. Silicon melts at 1414°C promoting mass transfer and higher SiC conversion. PCS+SiC coating showed higher weight retention and lower shrinkage than PCS alone. Preform shrinkage tracked dimensionally through 400°C, 1000°C, and 1450°C heat treatments. Porous rectangular samples showed ~14.6% average weight loss versus ~1% for solid disks. Filler dissolution in acetone introduced secondary porosity prior to infiltration, increasing average coating weight percentage from 16.9% to 26.8%.

notes: Paper describes stereolithographic additive manufacturing of three preceramic polymers via thiol-ene click chemistry: (1) polysiloxane SPR212 -> SiOC, (2) polycarbosilane SMP10 -> SiC(O), (3) polycarbosilazane Durazane 1800 -> SiCN(O). Oxygen contamination occurred in SMP10 and Durazane 1800 due to AM processing in ambient air reacting with Si-H and Si-N-Si bonds. Ceramic yield percentage not explicitly reported. notes: Study is bioinspired by Alitta virens marine worm jaw, where Zn2+ coordinates histidine-rich proteins to achieve high mechanical properties. Pyridine moieties installed on two commercial Si-based polymers (SMP-877 polycarbosilane from Starfire Systems; poly(mercaptopropyl)methylsiloxane from Gelest) via thiol-ene click chemistry using AIBN initiator at 70°C. Three metal chloride cross-linkers tested: ZnCl2, TiCl4, YCl3. Molar ratios expressed as polymer chains:metal ions. Coordination confirmed by ATR-FTIR shifts in pyridine ring absorptions (1380-1680 cm-1). Ti4+ coordinates more pyridine units per ion than Zn2+. Ceramic yield determined by TGA to 800°C; full pyrolysis at 1400°C/1h/argon in graphite furnace. XPS used for atomic composition of pyrolyzed ceramics. YCl3 cross-linking briefly characterized in supplementary information. Molecular weight of SMP-877 by GPC = 5000 g/mol; PMPS average 5500 g/mol used (range 4000-7000 g/mol).
source: Bioinspired cross-linking of preceramic polymers via metal ion coordination bonding

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Pyrolysis weight loss ranges from 64.6 to 74.9 wt-% depending on wood species. Stepwise decomposition: hemicellulose 200-260C, cellulose 240-350C, lignin 280-500C and above. Carbon yield ~90% at 600C. Slow heating rate of ~1C/min up to 400-500C required to avoid cracking; then 10-20C/min. Final pyrolysis temperatures in excess of 800C. Carbon yield 25-30 wt-% relative to initial wood mass.

Si content in final composite ranges from 10 to 67 wt-% depending on wood precursor.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Flexural/biaxial strength of porous SiC ceramics from wood-derived templates: 4-21 MPa (biaxial, Table 2). Flexural strength of dense bioSiC from various wood precursors ranges from ~50 to ~480 MPa depending on species and direction (Table 3). KIC ranges from ~0.46 to ~4.3 MPa·m^0.5. Elastic modulus ranges from ~1 to ~1410 MPa (likely GPa for dense materials per Table 3 context). Values are for final SiC ceramics, not the preceramic polymer.

notes: This paper is a review of biomorphic SiC ceramics derived from wood precursors, not a preceramic polymer study. No preceramic polymer is described. SiC is formed by melt infiltration of liquid Si into the carbon preform at >1450C in vacuum, or alternatively by SiO vapor infiltration or carbothermal reduction of SiO2 sol-gel precursors. notes: Resin used as preceramic DIW feedstock filled with 40 vol% hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) nanoplatelets (nominal particle size 500 nm, density 2.1 g/cc, median agglomerate size d50=4.5 µm). Printed flexural bars showed linear shrinkage of 6.4 ± 0.2% along print direction and 7.5 ± 0.6% transverse after tube furnace pyrolysis; unfilled resin reported at 25% linear shrinkage. notes: Polymer synthesized via two-step route: hydroboration of dichloromethylvinylsilane with borane dimethylsulfide, followed by aminolysis with methylamine. Glass transition temperature Tg ~38 C. Polymer yield 96%. Molecular formula per repeat unit [C12H30N3BSi3]n (MW 311.46 per unit). Melt-spinning performed in nitrogen atmosphere through 0.2 mm capillary spinneret. Curing in ammonia-nitrogen (70:30) proceeds in two stages: 25-70 C at 25 C/h held 2 h, then 70-200 C at 15 C/h held 2 h (~15 h total). Polymer is sensitive to moisture and air. O content <2 wt% in polymer (omitted from formula). Heating rate for pyrolysis to 1000 C was 50 C/h (~0.83 C/min); to 1400 C was 100 C/h (~1.67 C/min). Fiber diameter ~23 micrometers. Reference polymer [B(C2H4SiCH3NH)3]n (ammonolyzed analog) had insufficient rheology for fiber processing due to high crosslinking from Si-H and N-H sites.

notes: This is a broad review article (encyclopedia entry) covering the PDC field generally, not a single polymer study. Polymer types discussed include polysilanes, polycarbosilanes, polysilazanes, polysilylcarbodiimides, polysiloxanes, and polyborosilazanes. The Yajima process converts poly(dimethylsilane) via Kumada rearrangement at 400°C to poly(methyl hydrido carbosilane), then melt-spun and pyrolyzed at 1100°C in argon to SiC fibers. PBS-Me (N-methylpolyborosilazane) synthesized from hexamethyldisilazane, SiCl4, and BCl3 yields SiBN3C after pyrolysis in N2 at 1200°C. Shaping methods include casting, fiber drawing, coating, injection molding, pressing, impregnation, and additive manufacturing (3D printing). Cross-linking occurs below 200°C typically. Characterization methods cited: HR-TEM, solid-state NMR, Raman, FTIR, XPS, SAXS, SEM, TEM, elemental analysis, TGA-DSC with evolved gas analysis. Grain size of 1-3 nm refers to nanodomains in amorphous PDC matrix, used as midpoint value of 2 nm.

Polymer was dissolved in isopropanol and blended with a sacrificial acrylate photopolymer (Standard Blend 3D, Fun-to-do) and ferrocene (0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 wt% relative to PSZ) for DLP additive manufacturing. Printed parts pyrolyzed at 1200°C/2h/1°C/min under N2. Ferrocene acted as both UV light absorber (for z-resolution control) and catalytic modifier promoting in-situ formation of turbostratic carbon, graphite, and β-SiC during pyrolysis. Linear shrinkage ~30% after pyrolysis. Oxygen contamination present due to ambient-condition printing. EMW absorption: SCN-0.5 showed best performance: EAB 4.57 GHz at 1.30 mm, RLmin 61.34 dB at 2.22 mm. Raman ID/IG ratios: SCN-0=1.23, SCN-0.5=0.99, SCN-1=1.41, SCN-1.5=1.52.
source: Enhanced electromagnetic microwave absorption properties of SiCN(Fe) ceramics produced by additive manufacturing via in-situ reaction of ferrocene

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Siliconized SiC (Si-SiC) fabricated by binder jet additive manufacturing and reactive silicon melt infiltration. SiC volume fraction 65% (parallelepiped) and 48% (U-shaped tubular). Silicon matrix with percolating SiC clusters (parallelepiped) or uniformly distributed SiC particles (tubular). Small regions of unreacted carbon and porosity present in parallelepiped samples. SiO2 scale identified as mainly alpha-cristobalite by Raman spectroscopy after high-temperature oxidation.

notes: This paper does not describe a preceramic polymer. It concerns siliconized silicon carbide (Si-SiC) ceramic composites fabricated by binder jet additive manufacturing and reactive silicon melt infiltration. A phenolic-based binder and resole-type phenolic resin were used as processing aids (pyrolyzed at 850°C for 30 min in N2, or 200°C cure in air), but these are not the subject of study as preceramic polymers. The study focuses on oxidation/corrosion behavior of Si-SiC in SOFC anode environments (38% H2O + 15% H2 + 47% N2 at 1000°C for 905 h) and microturbine exhaust environments (~3-4 vol% H2O at ~634°C for 1000 and 2000 h). Oxide scale (SiO2, alpha-cristobalite) thickness: 7.7 ± 0.5 µm after SOFC exposure; 318 ± 9 nm at 642°C after 1000 h microturbine exposure. SiC powder: F500, d50 = 16.1 µm; nominal composition SiC 99.2 wt%, C 0.2 wt%, SiO2 0.3 wt%, Si 0.3 wt%. Silicon melt infiltration at 1450°C (30 min vacuum) then 1670°C (4 h, argon) for parallelepiped; 1450°C (30 min, <0.1 Pa vacuum) for tubular specimens.
source: Environmental stability of additively manufactured siliconized silicon carbide for applications in hybrid energy systems

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Binder jetted ceramic sand particles infiltrated with epoxy resin; silica porosity 40.1%, zirconia porosity 37.2%

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Infiltrated systems showed compressive and flexural strength one order of magnitude higher than non-infiltrated printed ceramic. Specific compressive strength: ~24 MPa·cm3/g for silica, ~21 MPa·cm3/g for zirconia. Non-infiltrated samples fractured below 5 MPa.

notes: This paper is NOT a preceramic polymer paper. It concerns binder-jetted ceramic sand molds (SiO2 and ZrO2) infiltrated with a commercial two-part epoxy resin (TC-1614 A/B, BJB Enterprises) for composite tooling applications. The epoxy is used as a structural infiltrant, not as a preceramic polymer. CTE of plain zirconia: 2.1 μm/m°C, plain silica: 14.28 μm/m°C, zirconia+epoxy: 69.14 μm/m°C, silica+epoxy: 75.96 μm/m°C, plain epoxy: 160.5 μm/m°C (all at 185°C). Particle sizes: silica ~175 μm, zirconia ~105 μm. Layer thickness: 280 μm. Curing protocol: stepwise from 66°C to 177°C. Thermostability tested up to 177°C for 10 cycles. No preceramic polymer chemistry is described.
source: Epoxy infiltrated 3D printed ceramics for composite tooling applications

notes: This paper is not about preceramic polymers. It describes solid-state interfacial reactions between boron nitride (BN) ceramic and titanium (Ti) metal at 1000-1200 degrees C, studying the formation of reaction zones containing TiB2, TiB, TiN1-x, Ti2N, and alpha-Ti(N) phases. No preceramic polymer content is present in this text.
source: Experimental study of the reaction zone at boron nitride ceramic–Ti metal interface

polymer_name: PBSZ (polyborosilazane); two variants: 15M (lower boron content) and 15MB (higher boron content)

elemental_composition.other_elements: B present; C content in pyrolysis products (NH3 atmosphere) less than 0.6 wt%; 15M-900C: B=2.4 wt%, Si=44.0 wt%; 15MB-900C: B=12.7 wt%, Si=34.7 wt%

bonding_structure.other_bonds: B-N bonds present (FTIR ~1400 cm-1); C-H bonds of Si-CH3 silyl methyl (2960, 2900 cm-1)

functional_groups.other: Si(H)-CH3 group identified by 1H-NMR at 0.3-0.45 ppm; B-N functional group

thermal_pyrolysis.pyrolysis_atmosphere: ammonia (NH3) for ceramic conversion; nitrogen and air for TGA
thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Sharp weight loss before 400°C; curves reach a peak after 800°C. Ceramic transformation of precursor completed at 800°C. TGA conducted from ambient to 900°C at 10°C/min in nitrogen and air. 15M ceramic yield in NH3 higher than 15MB. C content in NH3 pyrolysis products less than 0.6 wt%, indicating effective decarbonization. Pyrolysis stages explored at 400, 600, 800, 1000, 1200, 1400, and 1600°C.

backbone_architecture.description: Low-viscosity liquid at room temperature; mixed local structures with broad spectral peaks indicating multiple chemical environments; possible molecular structure shown with random repeat units m, n, p; synthesized from methylhydrodichlorosilane, boron trichloride, and hexamethyldisilazane

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Stable amorphous SiBN structure at 1400°C, mainly composed of B-N and Si-N bonds. Both 15M and 15MB had similar structural composition. Higher boron content led to more amorphous structures with increasing temperature.

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: XRD characterization performed with Cu Kα radiation (0.154 nm, 40 kV, 40 mA); specific phases not enumerated in extracted text

notes: Two precursor variants studied: 15M (lower boron content) and 15MB (higher boron content). Both synthesized from methylhydrodichlorosilane, boron trichloride, and hexamethyldisilazane in N-hexane. Mw=7142 and PDI=3.66 cited from reference [22] for PBSZ. Oxidation resistance tested in muffle furnace under air; mass retention data provided at 700, 900, 1200°C for oxidation tests. Higher boron content improved thermo-oxidative stability but worsened moisture stability. C content reduced to <0.6 wt% after NH3 pyrolysis. Elemental contents determined by ICP-OES. XRD range: 10-80° 2theta, step 0.026°, scan speed 2°/min. SEM and TEM used for microstructural characterization.
source: ExperimentalInvestigationsintothePyrolysisMechanismand CompositionofCeramicPrecursorsContainingBoronand NitrideswithDifferentBoronContents

notes: This paper is not about preceramic polymers. It concerns extrusion-based additive manufacturing of Ti-6Al-4V alloy parts using bimodal nano/microparticle powders produced by electric explosion of wire (EEW). The polymer binder used is a non-preceramic composition (EVA copolymer 10 wt%, tall oil rosin 75 wt%, dioctyl adipate 15 wt%) serving only as a sacrificial binder in a metal injection molding-like process. No preceramic polymer descriptors are applicable.
source: Extrusion-Based Additive Manufacturing of the Ti6Al4V Alloy Parts

elemental_composition.other_elements: Silicon, carbon, and oxygen detected via STEM EDS in the ceramic product; no quantitative atomic percentages reported

bonding_structure.other_bonds: C=C (alkene) present in preceramic polymer; Si-O, C-O, and Si-C peaks appear upon high-temperature conversion per FTIR; OH and C-H bonds present in polymer state

functional_groups.other: alkene groups noted; silane groups noted

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: TGA of polymer constituents performed; ceramic yield of ~80 wt% reported upon high-temperature pyrolysis at >=800°C; FTIR confirms disappearance of OH, C-H, Si-H, C=C bonds and appearance of Si-O, C-O, Si-C peaks indicating amorphous SiC-based ceramic conversion

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal - cross-linking via hydrosilylation, dehydrocoupling, and oxidation pathways; cured at 160°C and 230°C (1 h each) at 1°C/min in vacuum oven

backbone_architecture.description: Commercially available polycarbosilane (SMP-10) used as SiC preceramic polymer; no explicit backbone architecture described

microstructural.ceramic_phase: amorphous SiC-based ceramic (SiOC implied by elemental detection of Si, C, O)
microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Amorphous polymer-derived SiC-based ceramic; silicon, carbon, and oxygen all detected via STEM EDS; described as amorphous SiC ceramic derived from PCS

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Plateau stress 224 MPa; densification strain 57%; energy absorbed 207 MPa per unit volume (0.9 nJ); full strain recovery up to 14% engineering strain (99.5% recovery at 200 MPa/14% strain); 65% strain recovery at 1000 MPa/48% strain; Young's modulus average 1.3 GPa over first three cyclic compression cycles

notes: SMP-10 polycarbosilane used as preceramic polymer blended with triblock copolymer pMBM (PMMA-b-PnBA-b-PMMA, Mw=64000 g/mol, PDI=1.19) and PMMA homopolymer (Mw=120000 g/mol) in 2-ethylhexanol solvent for soft templating. Wormlike micelles (~13 nm width) formed only in presence of PCS. After pyrolysis at 800°C/argon, nanocoral ceramic structure formed with ~20 nm strut thickness and ~100-500 nm strut length (average 200 nm). Mesopores derived from wormlike micelle removal. Thermal cure step at 230°C prior to pyrolysis. Ceramic yield ~80 wt% stated for SMP-10 at >=800°C. Molecular weight and PDI values reported are for the as-received SMP-10 PCS (Mw=7500 g/mol, PDI=8.60).
source: Fabricating Ceramic Nanostructures with Ductile-like Compression Behavior via Rapid Self-Assembly of Block Copolymer and Preceramic Polymer Blends

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: At 1700 deg C: alpha-Si3N4 + beta-Si3N4 + minor Gd2SiO5, Si2NO2, AlSi0.5O2.5. At 1750 deg C: mostly beta-Si3N4. At 1800 deg C and above: single beta-Si3N4 phase. Addition of BNNTs does not influence alpha-to-beta phase transformation.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Fracture toughness of Si3N4 without BNNTs at 1800 deg C: 7.2 MPa m^1/2. Fracture toughness with 0.8 wt% BNNTs at 1800 deg C: 10.4 MPa m^1/2. Flexural strength decreases from 860 MPa to 711 MPa with increasing BNNTs content (0 to 1.2 wt%). Fracture toughness at 1.2 wt% BNNTs: 8.8 MPa m^1/2.

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: beta-Si3N4 (JCPDS No. 33-1160), alpha-Si3N4 (JCPDS No. 09-0250) at lower temperatures, Gd2SiO5 (JCPDS No. 40-0287), Si2NO2 (JCPDS No. 47-1627), AlSi0.5O2.5 (JCPDS No. 29-0084) at 1700 deg C

notes: This paper is NOT about preceramic polymers. It concerns the fabrication of silicon nitride (Si3N4) ceramics reinforced with boron nitride nanotubes (BNNTs) via hot-pressing sintering. No preceramic polymer is described. Sintering conditions: 1700-1850 deg C, 30 MPa nitrogen pressure, 1 h hold time. Additives: Al2O3 (6 wt%) and Gd2O3 (4 wt%) as sintering aids. BNNTs content varied from 0 to 1.2 wt%. Optimum sintering temperature: 1800 deg C. Most fields are null because this study does not involve preceramic polymer chemistry.
source: Fabrication and mechanical properties of boron nitride nanotube reinforced silicon nitride ceramics

polymer_name: PCS (Polycarbosilane, Suzhou Saifei Group Co., Ltd., China)

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: TGA was performed on the green SiC ceramic body (35 vol% solid loading) in N2 at 2 deg C/min up to 1000 deg C to characterize polymer binder burnout behavior. Polymer additives burnt out between 200-600 deg C; exothermic DTA peak at 38 deg C attributed to water vaporization. Polymer fully removed above 600 deg C. This TGA was for the resin/dispersant binders, not for PCS directly.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal - PCS-DVB precursor solution cured at 60 deg C for 1 h prior to pyrolysis

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: XRD confirmed pyrolyzed PCS converts to 6H-SiC phase (Card 74-1302). Final SiC ceramics from 30, 35, and 40 vol% slurries all identified as 6H-SiC.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Bending strength of final SiC ceramics after 8 PIP cycles: 142.1 MPa (30 vol%), 204.6 MPa (35 vol%), 184.2 MPa (40 vol%). Porous preform strength after polymer burnout: 15.2, 14.5, 14.1 MPa for 30, 35, 40 vol% respectively. Green strength: 28.7, 26.0, 24.0 MPa for 30, 35, 40 vol% respectively.

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: 6H-SiC (Card 74-1302)

notes: PCS was used as a preceramic polymer dissolved in Di-Vinyl-Benzene (DVB) as solvent at a PCS:DVB ratio of 1:0.5 (wt/wt). The PIP process was repeated 8 cycles. Final relative densities after 8 PIP cycles: 79.2% (30 vol%), 84.8% (35 vol%), 82.6% (40 vol%). Full densification was not achieved. The paper focuses on stereolithography additive manufacturing of SiC using PCS as PIP precursor; detailed characterization of PCS polymer itself (molecular weight, bonding structure, elemental composition) is not provided.
source: Fabrication of SiC ceramic architectures using stereolithography combined with precursor infiltration and pyrolysis

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Pure SiC matrix deposited by CVI using methyltrichlorosilane (MTS) precursor at 1000 °C; SiC whisker-reinforced SiC matrix composite (SiCW/SiC)

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Fracture toughness: 3.4 MPa·m^1/2 (SENB method); SiCW modulus reported as >550 GPa; elastic modulus of SiC matrix measured by nanoindentation at 9 mN for 2 s

notes: This paper does not describe a preceramic polymer. It describes fabrication of SiC whisker-reinforced SiC ceramic matrix composites (SiCW/SiC) using spray drying, binder jetting (3D printing), and chemical vapor infiltration (CVI). The CVI precursor is methyltrichlorosilane (MTS, CH3SiCl3) with H2 carrier and Ar diluent gas (ratio 1:40:40), total pressure 5000 Pa, deposition temperature 1000 °C, deposition times ranging from 120 to 840 h. SiCW volume fraction in preform: 17.7 vol.%. Open porosity decreased from 82.3 vol.% to ~1 vol.% with densification; closed porosity reached 11.4 vol.% at maximum densification. Two-stage pore structure: inter-particle pores 10–20 μm, intra-particle pores 1–3 μm. Toughening mechanisms observed: whisker pull-out, crack deflection, whisker bridging, crack branching. Fracture mode was brittle. No preceramic polymer is involved; most fields are not applicable.
source: Fabrication of SiC whisker-reinforced SiC ceramic matrix composites based on 3D printing and chemical vapor infiltration technology

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Intermediate dwell at 500 C for 30 min to remove gases forming during heating of SMP-10 prior to final pyrolysis at 1000 C for 1 h. Multiple infiltration and pyrolysis cycles performed (up to 6 cycles).

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: SMP-10 polycarbosilane converts to SiC upon pyrolysis; used to infiltrate SiCf/SiC composite preforms produced by binder jetting. Highest density achieved was 2.52 g/cm3 after six PIP cycles.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Hardness (Hv) and fracture toughness (K1C) reported for composite samples: irregular SiC powder: Hv = 11.6 GPa, K1C = 3.58 MPa·m^1/2; spherical SiC powder: Hv = 20.8 GPa, K1C = 6.13 MPa·m^1/2. These are composite properties, not polymer properties.

notes: This paper primarily focuses on binder jetting of SiCf/SiC ceramic matrix composites using SMP-10 (StarPCS polycarbosilane) as the infiltrant for polymer infiltration and pyrolysis (PIP). Very limited characterization data is provided for the SMP-10 polymer itself. The polymer is used as received from Starfire Systems. Infiltration was conducted in vacuum for 1 h. Up to 6 PIP cycles were performed. Young's modulus assumed as 360 GPa for fracture toughness calculation. The paper does not report ceramic yield, TGA data, molecular weight, or bonding structure of SMP-10.
source: Fabrication of Silicon Carbide Fiber-Reinforced Silicon Carbide Matrix Composites Using Binder Jetting Additive Manufacturing from Irregularly-Shaped and Spherical Powders

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Alpha-Si3N4 (PDF:09-0250) present after nitridation at 1500C; transforms predominantly to beta-Si3N4 (PDF:09-2059) after sintering at 1700C; liquid phase Y2(Si3O3N4) (PDF:88-0213) forms at 1750C; excessive sintering at 1800C causes partial glass phase disappearance and beta-Si3N4 grain fracture. Starting powder was 91 wt% Si3N4 (93 wt% alpha, 7 wt% beta), 5 wt% Y2O3, 3 wt% Al2O3, 1 wt% PVA.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Bending strength of 41.5 MPa reported for the Si:Si3N4=50:50 sample sintered at 1750C (this work). Adding Si powder at 50:50 ratio enhanced bending strength by 2.9x at 1750C and 2.5x at 1800C compared to no Si addition. Porosity >40% for all BJ-printed samples.

notes: This paper is NOT about preceramic polymers. It concerns binder jetting 3D printing of porous Si3N4 ceramics using Si and Si3N4 powder mixtures with epoxy resin as the printing binder. The epoxy resin binder is removed by decarbonization prior to nitridation and sintering; it is not a preceramic polymer. Precursor infiltration pyrolysis (PIP) is mentioned only as a comparison method from prior literature. Real permittivity (epsilon prime) of the final ceramic was consistently below 3.3. Minimum porosity achieved was 47.24% (S1750-4-50-50, density 1.60 g/cm3). Nitridation performed at 1500C for 2h to convert Si to Si3N4; pressureless sintering at 1700-1800C for 4h. All preceramic polymer fields are null as this paper does not describe a preceramic polymer.
source: Fabrication of broadband wave-transparent porous Si3N4 ceramics by powder hybrid mechanism combined with binder jetting 3D technology

polymer_name: poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate (PEGDA) with phenyl bis(2,4,6-trimethylbenzoyl)phosphine oxide photoinitiator

bonding_structure.other_bonds: Acrylate C=C bonds that undergo photopolymerisation upon UV exposure at 380 nm; ester linkages in PEGDA backbone

functional_groups.other: Diacrylate end groups; ethylene glycol repeat units; phosphine oxide photoinitiator

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: TGA run from 50 to 600 C at 5 C/min in flowing air (25 ml/min). Volatile solvent evaporates in 140-200 C range. Resin decomposes in two exothermic steps: first peak at 375 C, second strongly exothermic peak at 480 C leaving 5-7% residual organic matter. Final residual mass approximately equals original ceramic loading mass fraction, indicating no significant solvent loss during post-processing.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: UV photopolymerisation at 380 nm (DLP projector); post-cure under 253 nm UV lamp for 2-4 min

backbone_architecture.description: Diacrylate monomer/oligomer system that forms a crosslinked polymer network upon UV-initiated free radical photopolymerisation; used as binder matrix loaded with 25-60 wt% ceramic powder (alumina, 3-YSZ, 8-YSZ)

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Alumina and 8-YSZ retained original phases after sintering. 3-YSZ started as 50:50 monoclinic/tetragonal mixture and evolved predominantly to tetragonal with some cubic peaks after sintering. 3D printing process does not affect phase stability relative to conventional processing.

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: Alumina (Al2O3); monoclinic and tetragonal ZrO2 (3-YSZ raw powder); tetragonal ZrO2 with minor cubic (3-YSZ sintered); cubic/tetragonal ZrO2 (8-YSZ)

notes: This paper is not primarily about a preceramic polymer. It describes a DLP stereolithography-based 3D printing process using poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate (PEGDA) as a photopolymerisable binder resin loaded with ceramic powders (alumina, 3-YSZ, 8-YSZ at 25-60 wt%). The resin is not a preceramic polymer; it burns out during sintering. Green bodies were dried at 60 C (6-12 h) then 140 C (3 h), then sintered at 1200-1500 C for 6 h at 5 C/min. For 8-YSZ, an alternative debinding step under 5% H2/Ar at 450 C for 6 h at 2 C/min was used to prevent cracking. Photogrammetry and Structure-from-Motion (SfM) were used to evaluate dimensional accuracy. Shrinkage in xy plane was 50-60% for 3- and 8-YSZ sintered at 1400-1500 C. Layer thickness during printing: 25-50 micrometers. UV exposure: 70-80 s for first 4 layers, 5-7 s for subsequent layers.
source: Fabricationandcharacterisationofceramicsvialow-costDLP3Dprinting

bonding_structure.other_bonds: C-H bonds noted; Si-H and C-H gas evolution reported during thermal decomposition up to 1500 C

functional_groups.other: allyl group (allylhydridopolycarbosilane)

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Ceramic yield calculated from crosslinked specimens; mass loss during cross-linking was 12-12.3%, making total ceramic yields about 10% lower than tabulated values. Ceramic yield decreases with increasing temperature and dwell time, and is lower in vacuum than in argon. Yields ranged from ~74.8% to ~90.1% depending on conditions. Thermal decomposition occurs up to 1500 C with evolution of C-H, Si-H and H2 gases.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal - cured at 300 C for 2 h at 5 C/min in box furnace under argon

backbone_architecture.description: Commercial allylhydridopolycarbosilane (AHPCS) liquid precursor supplied by Starfire Systems (SMP-10)

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Beta-SiC is the major phase in all conditions. Minor graphite peaks detected, especially in argon atmosphere; graphite peaks decrease with increasing temperature and dwell time due to carbothermal reduction of oxide impurities. Random stacking faults observed as plateau on left side of (111) XRD peak. SiOC amorphous phase separates into SiO2, SiC and C above 1300 C. EDS data shows Si, C, and O present in pyrolyzed samples.

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: beta-SiC (major), graphite (minor)

notes: Paper focuses on pyrolysis of AHPCS (SMP-10) using spark plasma sintering (SPS) vs. tube furnace. SPS heating rate was 50 C/min vs. 5 C/min for tube furnace. Pyrolysis temperatures ranged from 1100-1500 C with dwell times of 0, 1, or 2 h under argon or vacuum. Crystallinity ranged from 25.05% (A11, 1100 C, no dwell, Ar) to 82.92% (V15D2, 1500 C, 2h dwell, vacuum). Crystallite sizes ranged from 1.1 nm to 11.2 nm. EDS elemental compositions (atomic%) for selected samples: A13D2 (Si=32.3, C=61.9, O=5.8), A14D2 (Si=57.4, C=39.4, O=3.2), A15D2 (Si=59.2, C=39.8, O=1.0), V13D2 (Si=37.3, C=57.0, O=5.7), V14D2 (Si=60.3, C=38.7, O=1.0), V15D2 (Si=60.8, C=38.4, O=0.8). Crosslinking at 300 C resulted in 12-12.3% mass loss. SPS-pyrolyzed PDC showed ~5% higher crystallinity than tube furnace at same conditions. Ceramic yield not strongly affected by heating method. Fast heating in vacuum caused sample cracking due to rapid gas evolution.
source: Fast pyrolysis of a SiC-based polymer precursor using a spark plasma sintering apparatus – Effects of heating methods and pyrolysis atmosphere

microstructural.ceramic_phase: SiC (beta 3C polytype in as-received powder; transforms to alpha 6H polytype after sintering at 2150 degrees C)
microstructural.phase_composition_notes: As-received powder is beta-SiC (3C). After sintering at 2150 degrees C, phase transformation to alpha-SiC (6H polytype) observed in all samples (45-56 vol% solids loading). Peak intensity and sharpness of alpha-SiC increased with solids loading, indicating enhanced crystallinity at higher packing densities.

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: beta-SiC (3C polytype) in as-received powder; alpha-SiC (6H polytype) after sintering at 2150 degrees C

notes: This paper does not describe a preceramic polymer. It describes direct ink writing (DIW) of SiC ceramic slurries using polyethyleneimine (PEI, 25k MW) as a dispersant in an aqueous colloidal suspension. The SiC powder (D50 ~446 nm, max <1.7 um) is a pre-formed ceramic powder, not a polymer-derived ceramic. Sintering was performed at 2150-2200 degrees C in pressureless conditions. Final sintered density reached ~93.5% theoretical density for 56 vol% formulation (3.01 g/cc). Solids loading ranged from 35 to 56 vol%; percolation threshold estimated at ~57 vol%. PEI was used only as a colloidal dispersant, not as a preceramic polymer. All preceramic polymer descriptor fields are null because no preceramic polymer is described in this work.
source: Feldbauer_2026_Maximizing solids loading for aqueous slurry robocasting of silicon carbide

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Flexural properties of Nicalon/SiC composites reported: transverse matrix fracture strength 150 MPa, ultimate flexure strength 325 MPa, work of fracture 65 J/m2; edge-on matrix fracture strength 150 MPa, ultimate flexure strength 425 MPa, work of fracture 127 J/m2. In-plane longitudinal moduli C11 130-248 GPa, through-thickness moduli C33 6-138 GPa.

notes: This paper does not describe a preceramic polymer. It concerns Nicalon-fiber reinforced SiC ceramic-matrix composites fabricated by forced chemical vapor infiltration (FCVI) using methyltrichlorosilane (CH3SiCl3) and hydrogen gas. No preceramic polymer is discussed. The Nicalon fiber composition is 58 wt% Si, 31 wt% C, 11 wt% O. All preceramic polymer fields are null because the subject matter is outside the scope of preceramic polymer chemistry.
source: Fiber-Reinforced CMCs_Processing,

bonding_structure.other_bonds: Polymer-derived ceramic matrix described as yielding microcrystalline Si-O-C-Fe-Cr-based ceramic upon pyrolysis; O-rich domains of oxycarbide glass matrix noted

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Volume porosity of pyrolyzed samples measured at 6%; linear shrinkage along fiber direction of 5.5% observed

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal - cross-linking at 240°C in air

backbone_architecture.description: Polymethylsilsesquioxane (T-type resin, RSiO1.5 repeat unit) used as preceramic precursor; loaded with FeSiCr (34 vol%) and SiC fillers (16 vol%)

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Microcrystalline Si-O-C-Fe-Cr-based ceramic composite described; O-rich domains of oxycarbide glass matrix noted; derived from FeSiCr/SiC-filled polymethylsilsesquioxane pyrolyzed at 1200°C in argon

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Fracture toughness KIC = 3 MPa·m^0.5; Fracture energy G = 48 J/m²; Poisson ratio = 0.2; Coefficient of thermal expansion = 7.95e-6 K^-1 (measured by dilatometry)

notes: The paper primarily concerns Ti3SiC2-coated SiC fiber-reinforced PDC composites; the preceramic polymer (Silres MK, polymethylsilsesquioxane, Wacker Chemie AG) is used as matrix precursor mixed with 34 vol% FeSiCr and 16 vol% SiC fillers. Warm-pressing at 80°C/0.2 MPa, crosslinking at 240°C in air, pyrolysis at 1200°C in argon. Matrix Young's modulus of 187 GPa refers to the final ceramic composite matrix. Fiber (SCS-6 SiC monofilament) E=380 GPa, Ti3SiC2 interlayer E=320 GPa. No detailed polymer molecular weight, elemental composition of the precursor, or ceramic yield data explicitly provided.
source: Filbert-Demut et al. - 2015 - Influence of Ti3SiC2 Fiber Coating on Interface and Matrix Cracking in an SiC Fiber-Reinforced Polym

elemental_composition.other_elements: Zirconia (ZrO2) and Alumina (Al2O3) nanoparticles; Zr, Al, O confirmed by EDX

bonding_structure.other_bonds: Acrylamide and N,N'-methylene bisacrylamide crosslinked polymer network; no silicon-based preceramic polymer bonds described

functional_groups.other: Acrylamide groups (from acrylamide and N,N'-methylene bisacrylamide); photoinitiator BA740 (2,5-Bis[4-[N,N-Bis-[2-(Acetyloxy)Ethyl]Phenyl]-Methylene]-(2E,5E)-Cyclopentanone)

thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Debinding performed between 325 and 375 C; sintering at 1450 C with 100 min dwell. Significant shrinkage of up to 50% observed during post-processing, particularly debinding and sintering.

notes: Study focuses on SiOC ceramic derived from polysiloxane precursors; three precursor systems used: 85PVMS/15PHMS, 85PMPS/15PHMS, and pure PSO. notes: This thesis investigates four manufacturing methods for BNNT-reinforced polysilazane-derived SiCN ceramic composites: (1) ball-milling mixing, (2) polymer infiltration and pyrolysis (PIP), (3) precursor mixing, and (4) ethanol mixing. Composite densities for pristine SiCN varied by method: ball-milling control 1.28 g/cm3, PIP SiCN film 2.03 g/cm3, precursor mixing 0 wt% ~comparable, ethanol mixing control 1.22 g/cm3. It concerns direct-ink-writing (DIW) 3D printing of porous SiC ceramics using SiC powder-based aqueous foam inks with organic additives (PVA, PEG, methyl cellulose as binder/dispersant, DTAB as foaming agent) and sintering aids (Al2O3, Y2O3, SiO2). SiC powder loading was 35 vol%. Ink storage modulus G' = 2.7 kPa, yield stress = 490 Pa. EM wave absorption: minimum reflection loss -48.9 dB, maximum effective absorption bandwidth 3.7 GHz. thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Specimens were pyrolyzed by ramping at 1 C/min up to 650 C and holding for 24 h to burn out organic binders before hot pressing. This is a binder burnout step, not a polymer-to-ceramic conversion.

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: Multi-phase carbide specimens with either discrete or continuous composition variation. B4C and SiC loaded at 47.5 vol% each in separate inks. Hot pressed at 35 MPa and 1950 C yielding near full density.

mechanical_properties.other_mechanical: Knoop hardness values of 20-23 GPa reported for hot-pressed specimens. B4C elastic modulus 483 GPa, Poisson ratio 0.17; SiC elastic modulus 411 GPa, Poisson ratio 0.16.

notes: This paper does not describe a preceramic polymer. It describes direct ink writing (DIW) of aqueous ceramic particulate suspensions (B4C and SiC powders) with polyethyleneimine (PEI) dispersant and methylcellulose (MC) binder. The inks are colloidal suspensions, not preceramic polymers. The pyrolysis step at 650 C is a binder burnout, not polymer-to-ceramic conversion. Final densification was by hot pressing at 35 MPa and 1950 C for 2 h. Hardness range 20-23 GPa; midpoint 21.5 GPa used. Hold time of 24 h = 1440 min for binder burnout. Hot pressing also included intermediate hold at 1350 C for 1 h. B4C CTE: 5.5e-6 /K; SiC CTE: 3.0e-6 /K.

bonding_structure.other_bonds: NH2 groups detected in PDPS by IR at 3560 cm-1; Si-Br bonds introduced during NH4Br-catalyzed polymerization of PDPS (subsequently removed by NH3 treatment)

thermal_pyrolysis.pyrolysis_atmosphere: N2, NH3 (wet and dry), Ar, vacuum
thermal_pyrolysis.tga_notes: Two-stage pyrolysis: 1100°C (alumina tube furnace, N2 at 120°C/h or NH3 at 300°C/h, hold 2h) then 1550°C (graphite furnace, 17°C/min, hold 3.5-4h). Ceramic yields at 1100°C ranged 19-73% depending on polymer and atmosphere. N2 pyrolysis gave black residues; NH3 pyrolysis gave white/grey residues. Weight losses at 1550°C ranged 3.1-87% depending on conditions. Wet NH3 (1250 ppm water) introduced Si-O character into residues. Black residues crystallized to SiC or Si3N4 only; white residues crystallized to Si3N4, Si2N2O, SiC, SiO2, and/or Si depending on conditions. Crucible material (alumina vs graphite) affected product distribution.

crosslink_density.crosslinking_method: thermal (PMSED solidified over 20 days, attributed to cross-linking with elimination of ethylenediamine; NH4Br-catalyzed polymerization for PDPS; NaNH2-initiated dehydropolymerization for PHMCS from HMCS)

backbone_architecture.description: PCS: polycarbosilane derived from thermolysis of poly(dimethyl)silane at ~470°C. HMCS: cyclic hydridomethylsilazane oligomer. PHMCS: higher MW polymer from dehydropolymerization of HMCS using NaNH2. PDPS: poly(diphenyl)silazane from NH4Br-catalyzed polymerization. PMSED: poly(methylsilylethylenediamine), initially low-viscosity oil solidifying over 20 days, possibly forming ladder/cross-linked network.

microstructural.phase_composition_notes: 1100°C residues amorphous (XRD broad/weak). 1550°C crystallization yields: beta-SiC (major) and alpha-Si3N4 from N2 pyrolysis; alpha-Si3N4 (major), beta-Si3N4, Si2N2O, SiC, SiO2, Si from NH3 pyrolysis depending on wet/dry gas, crucible type (alumina or graphite), and second-stage atmosphere (N2, Ar, vacuum). Black residues (from N2 pyrolysis) yielded only SiC or Si3N4; white residues (from NH3 pyrolysis) yielded complex mixtures including Si2N2O. White amorphous residues characterized as silicon oxycarbonitrides (SixNyOzCa); black residues as silicon carbonitrides (SixNyCz).

conformation_crystallinity.xrd_phases_identified: alpha-SiC, beta-SiC (mixture of polytypes), alpha-Si3N4, beta-Si3N4, Si2N2O, SiO2 (cristobalite), Si

notes: Study involves five preceramic polymers: PCS (polycarbosilane, precursor to SiC), HMCS (hydridomethylcyclosilazane), PHMCS (poly(hydridomethylcyclosilazane)), PDPS (poly(diphenyl)silazane), PMSED (poly(methylsilylethylenediamine)) - the latter four are polysilazane precursors to Si3N4. PCS prepared from (CH3)2SiCl2 via thermolysis of PDMS at ~470°C in Ar (34-69 bar). PDPS from (C6H5)2SiCl2 ammonolysis then NH4Br polymerization. HMCS from CH3SiHCl2 and NH3. PHMCS by NaNH2 dehydropolymerization of HMCS in THF. PMSED from CH3SiHCl2 and ethylenediamine. 29Si MAS NMR: N2-pyrolyzed black residues show broad peak at -14.5 ppm (PCS, amorphous SiC character) or -29.8 to -50 ppm (polysilazanes, SiC/Si3N4/Si2N2O environments); wet NH3 residues show peaks at -45 to -53.7 ppm (Si3N4-type) and -87.9 to -99.9 ppm (SiO2-type); dry NH3 reduces SiO2-associated peaks. Crucible choice (alumina vs graphite) significantly affected crystalline product distribution at 1550°C. Relative alpha/beta-Si3N4 proportions calculated by XRD peak height method (Gazzara and Messier). Ceramic yield for HMCS in N2 increased from 33.3% to 73.3% upon polymerization to PHMCS. 1100°C heating rates: 120°C/h (N2), 300°C/h (NH3). 1550°C heating rate: 17°C/min. Ceramic yield range at 1100°C: 19-73%.
source: NMR and X-ray diffraction studies of amorphous and crystallized pyrolysis residues from pre-ceramic polymers

notes: This paper is not about a preceramic polymer. With initiator, weight loss starts above 350C due to condensation of gaseous ammonia. Pyrolysis starts above 400C with elimination of methane, ethylene, and hydrogen. Further shrinkage above 800C due to residual hydrogen release. Crystallization initiated at higher temperatures depending on composition and atmosphere.
